caption: You start with the king pawn going forward. A great first move that grabs the center and opens lines for your pieces.
Your opponent copies you. This is a calm, equal start. Just keep developing your pieces toward the center.
You bring out your knight and attack the e5 pawn. Good, fast development — this is the right idea.
They play d6 to guard the pawn instead of the more active Nc6. This is a bit passive, so you get a small edge. Keep building in the center.

You aim your bishop at f7, the weak spot near their king. A fine attacking spot, though the engine liked pushing d4 to grab more center. Lesson: in open games, taking the center with d4 is often even stronger than a quick bishop move.
They pin nothing real and just put the bishop on g4. You can simply play h3 next to ask the bishop a question. Small gift for you.
You support e4 with d3. It is solid, but d4 was better because it claims more space in the middle. Lesson: when you can play d4 safely, the bigger center usually pays off.
They develop the knight to f6 — a normal, good move. Nothing to fear; just keep getting ready to castle.
You pin their knight with the bishop. Castling first was a touch better and safer. Lesson: getting your king to safety early avoids surprises.
They poke your bishop with h6. Just keep the bishop alive on the diagonal — no harm done.
You slide the bishop back to h4 and keep the pin. A clean, equal move that holds the tension.
They push g5, gaining space but weakening their king's home. Note this — their king will be airy later. Keep developing.
You retreat the bishop to g3, the best square, eyeing their weak dark squares. Calm and correct.
They put the knight on c6 instead of finishing development. This lets you grab a small edge. Get your pieces out and watch the center.
Nc3 lets their knight jump to d4 and cause trouble; c3 was much better to stop that hop. Lesson: before developing, check if a square like d4 is open for the enemy knight — control it first.
They land the knight on d4, the strong square you left open. Stay calm; you can challenge it or trade it off soon.
You play h3 to bother the g4 bishop. It is fine, almost equal. Keep your king's plans in mind.
They trade the knight for yours on f3, handing you the two bishops. Recapture with gxf3 — your pawns get doubled but your bishops are strong and lines open.
You take back with the pawn. Good — your rook file opens up and your bishops are a real asset now.
They drop the bishop to h5, pinning your f3 pawn. Not scary; just continue your plan in the center with d4 soon.
Qe2 is okay, but d4 was stronger to open the middle while you have the two bishops. Lesson: when you own the bishop pair, opening the position makes them even better.
They play a6, a slow move that weakens their queenside. Now d4 or h4 to open lines looks great for you. Keep pressing.
You castle long, tucking your king away and connecting rooks. Solid choice — now your rooks can join the attack.
Qd7 is a weak square for the queen and helps you. The engine shows d4 next is strong, cracking open the center. Strike in the middle!
You finally play d4, hitting the center hard. Exactly right — this opens lines toward their king.
They take on d4, opening the d-file straight at their own queen and king. Recapture with Rxd4 — your rook gets active and points at the danger zone.
Rxd4 grabs the open file with power. Your rook now eyes their king side — great attacking setup.
They castle long into the same side as your attack — risky for them. The engine shows Bxa6 wins material by ripping open their king. Take it!
You play Bxa6, smashing the pawn cover in front of their king. Perfect — this opens the b-file for a deadly attack.
They recapture with the b-pawn, but this opens the door to a forced mate. Play Qxa6+ at once — checks lead straight to checkmate.
Qxa6+ starts the finishing blow. The king must move and you are now hunting it down with check after check.
They run the king to b8 — the only square, but it cannot escape. Now Rb4+ brings the rook in for the kill.
Rb4+ delivers the knockout check; after they block with Qb5, you play Rxb5 mate. Beautiful finish — you opened lines and chased the king to mate. Well played!
You start with the king pawn going forward. This is a great, classic first move that grabs the center.
Your opponent copies you with their king pawn. This is the open game — fight for the center now with knights coming out.
Your knight jumps out and attacks their e5 pawn. Strong, normal developing move.
They guard the pawn with d6 instead of the more active Nc6. This is a quiet, slightly passive setup — you have free time to build the center with d4.
Your bishop comes out aiming at their f7 weak spot. Good, but pushing d4 to take the center was even better here.
They play h6 to stop your pieces landing on g5. This wastes a move — grab the center now with d4.
You support your e4 pawn with d3. Safe, but d4 (taking more center) was the stronger plan.
Their bishop pins your knight to your queen. Just kick it with h3 — they must decide to take or step back.
Your knight develops and adds a guard to e4. Fine, though h3 to ask the pinning bishop was a touch better.
They bring the knight out to attack your bishop's diagonal. Calm down with h3 to deal with their g4 bishop.
You play a3, but this does little. Better was Be3 to develop and prepare to challenge their knight; a3 lets them jump to d4.
Their knight leaps to d4, a strong central post. Meet it with Be3 to develop and contest the squares.

BIG MISTAKE. You gave up your bishop with Bxf7+ but it wins nothing — after Kxf7 you are just down a bishop. The quiet Be3 kept the game even. Lesson: only sacrifice when you see a clear follow-up that wins back more.
They take your bishop with the king, as expected. You are now down material — play solid moves like Be3 and try to make their king feel unsafe.
Another bad sacrifice — Nxe5+ throws away your knight for a pawn. Be3 was steady. Lesson: a check that loses a piece for nothing only makes things worse.
They take your knight with the pawn. You are now down a lot of material — at least grab their bishop next with Qxg4.
Their knight forks with check and grabs your c2 pawn. Step away calmly — Kd2 was best, keeping your pieces tighter.
Kf1 is a mistake; the king goes to a worse square. Kd2 was better and kept things together. Now their knight can grab your rook in the corner.
They take your rook in the corner with Nxa1 — a big grab, but that knight is now trapped far away. Hit back fast with Qh5+ to start chasing their king.
Qf5+ checks, but Qh5+ was sharper to harass the king. Still, you keep their king walking.
They block with the queen on f6. You can keep the pressure — Qh5+ keeps checking and probing their king.
Qd7+ keeps checking and pins them down. Qh5+ was a bit stronger, but you are still bothering their king.
They block with Qe7, forced. Keep going — Qd5+ next forces them again and eyes their loose pawns.
Qd5+ checks and lines up to win their b7 pawn. Good, exactly the engine's plan.
They block with Qe6 again, forced. Now collect the pawn with Qxb7.
You snap up the b7 pawn with the queen. Nice — you are clawing material back.
They develop the rook to d8 and offer a queen trade. Just keep improving; pushing f4 to wake up your pieces was the idea.
Nd5 is okay but f4 (activating your side) was sharper. Your knight does jump to a strong central spot though.
Their bishop comes to d6. You can keep developing — Be3 brings out your last piece and eyes their a7 pawn.
h4 gains space on the side and opens a path for your rook. Solid, the engine liked it.
They play Ne7 to challenge your strong d5 knight. Activate your rook with Rh3, swinging it toward their king.
Rh3 lifts the rook so it can swing across to attack. Excellent, top engine move.
They trade knights on d5. Recapture with exd5 — your pawn now sits strong in the center.
You recapture with the pawn, gaining a nice central pawn. Good and correct.
They put the queen on d7. You can check with Rf3+ to push their king around.
Rf3+ gives a check. Quietly building with b3 was a hair better, but the check still pesters their king.
They walk the king up to g6 — this is risky and exposes the king. Punish it with Rg3+ to drive the king and attack.
Qxa7 grabs a pawn, but you missed g4, which builds a real attack on the open king. Material is nice, but the attack was bigger.
They bring the other rook to f8. Their king on g6 is still exposed — check with Rg3+ to chase it.
Rg3+ checks and pushes their king back. Good — keep hunting that exposed king.
They run the king to h7, forced. Keep coordinating — Qe3 brings the queen toward the attack.
Qe3 centralizes your queen for the attack. Strong, the engine fully approved.
Their knight escapes to c2. Hit them with Qe4+, a check that also keeps your pieces active.
Qe4+ checks and centralizes with power. Good, top choice.
They block with Qf5 and offer a queen trade. Pushing h4-h5 to keep the attack going was the idea.
Qe2 retreats and is a little passive; b4 was more useful. Not terrible, but you lost some pressure.
They push e4 to open lines and free their bishop. Be careful — this opens an attack on your rook on the g-file.
MISTAKE. Qxc2 grabs the knight but drops your rook — Rxg7+ was a strong check first. Lesson: when both sides have threats, check or capture with tempo before grabbing material.
They take your rook with Bxg3. You lost the exchange — steady yourself with Be3 and hold things together.
dxe4 is a mistake; Be3 was needed to stay solid. Now their queen and bishop get dangerous near your king.
They miss the strong Qxf2+ and instead play Qf6. Lucky for you — bring out Be3 to defend and stay in the game.
e5+ gives a check with your pawn and offers a queen trade. Good — this is the engine's top move.
They block with Qf5 instead of trading. Now trade queens with Qxf5+ — it simplifies and eases the pressure.
HUGE BLUNDER. Qd2 hangs everything — you had to play Qxf5+ to trade queens and survive. Lesson: when a piece is being attacked or a trade saves you, deal with it before doing anything else.
You start with the King's Pawn opening — a great first move that takes the center. Nice start.
Your opponent meets you head-on for a classic Open Game. Just keep developing your pieces.
You bring out your knight to attack the e5 pawn and develop. Perfect.
They defend the pawn with their knight. Both sides are playing the book moves well.
This is the Italian Game, a strong setup. Your bishop aims right at the f7 weak spot near their king.
They develop their knight and eye your e4 pawn. Keep an eye on that pawn.
You quietly guard e4 with the pawn. Solid and safe, though the sharp Ng5 was also possible.
They push h6 to stop your knight jumping to g5. A small waste of time; just keep building up.
You develop your last knight. Fine, but c3 to prepare a big center with d4 was a touch better.
They tuck the bishop on e7. A bit passive — the active Bc5 was stronger for them.
You place your bishop on e3, eyeing their side. Reasonable, but pushing a3 first to stop Bb4 was cleaner.
They play b6 to fianchetto their bishop, but this is loose. You can grab space with a3 and Bd5 ideas.
You play a3 to stop their bishop coming to b4. A useful little move, though d4 to hit the center was best.
They put the bishop on the long line aiming at your king side. Watch that bishop's aim at g2 later.
You grab queenside space with b4. Active, but calmly finishing with Qd2 and castling was safer.
Big mistake by them — d5 drops a pawn. Just take it: exd5 wins material cleanly.
You take the pawn. Excellent — this was the best move and you are now ahead.
They jump the knight to d4 hoping for tricks, but it doesn't quite work. Grab the e5 pawn with Nxe5.
You take the free e5 pawn. Great choice — you are winning material.
Another blunder — c5 loses more. The crushing reply is dxc6, opening lines and winning a piece.
You play dxc6, exactly right. You are now far ahead.
They recapture with the bishop. You have a strong attack brewing on f7.
You grab f7 with the knight, forking and winning more. The bishop check first was a hair better, but this is still winning.
They defend with the queen. Stay calm and keep collecting material.
You snatch the rook in the corner — a huge material grab. Keeping the knight active with Ne5 was even stronger, but you are crushing.
They grab your g2 pawn with the bishop, as that long-aimed bishop always wanted. No worry — you are still way ahead.
They take your rook in the corner. The material is still hugely in your favor.
You play Bb5 to trade off their dangerous bishop. Smart and accurate.
They block with Bc6 to offer the trade. Good — take it and simplify.
You trade bishops. Right idea — fewer pieces means your extra material wins easier.
They recapture with the queen. Keep your pieces safe and push your winning edge.
Careless — b5 lets their queen get active. Bringing your knight out with Ng6 kept things clean and winning.
They retreat the queen to d7. You're fine; reorganize and stay solid.
You play Qf3 to get your queen active and safe. Good, this was the best move.
They swing the rook to the open c-file. Watch that rook — it can become annoying near your king.
Castling here is a serious blunder — it walks into Bxa3+ and lets their attack roar to life. The calm Ne2 kept your king safe and your win intact.
They correctly check with Bxa3+ and grab a pawn. You must respond carefully now — your king is exposed.
You step the king to d2, the best square. Stay very alert; your king is in the open.
Re1+ rushes in but misfires. Quietly playing Ne2 to shield your king was far stronger.
They step the king to f8. You still have chances, but tread carefully.
You check with Ng6+. Fine, it keeps them busy.
They move the king to g8. Look for a way to cover your own king now.
Ne7+ gives away your knight without enough gain. Tucking your king to e2 was the safe path.
They take your knight with the bishop. Material is slipping, and your king is bare.
You take the bishop back with the rook. Okay, but the danger to your king is growing.
They check and grab your c3 pawn. Your king is getting chased — stay accurate.
You step to e2, the right square. Keep finding the safe squares.
They grab the c2 pawn with check. Your pawns are falling and the king is very open.
You go to f1, exactly right. Keep dodging the checks.
They check from b1. Just keep walking the king to safety.
You go to g2, the best square. Hang in there — keep the king tucked.
They lift the rook to c1 to add pressure. The threats are mounting; defend very carefully.
Qa8+ chases the wrong way and lets them swing back. The active Qf5 kept you in the fight.
They calmly block with the king to h7. Now their attack is real — you must defend with great care.
This is the losing move — grabbing the a7 pawn ignores the deadly check coming. You had to play Qc6 to defend; now mate is near.
They check with Rg1+ and the net closes. Your king has almost no escape left.
You step to f3, the only move. There is no good defense remaining.
They grab d3 with check, pulling the queen in for the kill. The end is coming.
You block with Re3, the forced try. Sadly it cannot stop the mate.
They check with Qd5+, setting up the finish. Nothing saves the king now.
You step to f4 with no choice left. Mate is unavoidable.
Rg4# ends the game. You played a brilliant winning game until your king got caught in the open — the big lesson is to keep your king safe before chasing more material.
White opens with the king pawn to grab the center. Be ready to fight for the middle too.
You answer in the center with your own pawn. This is a classic, solid start.
White's knight comes out and pokes at your e5 pawn. You need to guard that pawn.
Nice — your knight develops and defends the e5 pawn at the same time. Lesson: try to make each move do two jobs.
White's bishop aims at the weak f7 square near your king. This is the Italian Game; watch f7.
Your bishop comes out and points at White's side too. This balanced setup is called the Giuoco Piano.
White castles and tucks the king away safely. A normal, calm move — keep developing.
Good — your knight develops and eyes the center. You are right on plan.
White plays a small pawn move to support the center. Nothing scary; carry on building.
A useful little move that stops a White piece from jumping to g5. Quiet and fine.
White's last knight comes out. No threat yet, just development.
Solid — your pawn move opens a path for your light bishop and supports e5. Perfect.
White spends a slow move on a pawn and wastes a little time. This is your chance to get active first.
Your bishop develops, but a6 was a touch better to control the b5 square and stop White's knight ideas. Lesson: when an enemy knight wants to jump in, a little pawn move can lock it out.
White's knight jumps to the edge to attack your dark bishop. Just move the bishop to safety.
Good — you slide the bishop back and keep it safe and useful. Exactly right.
White trades knight for your bishop. Take back and you fix your pawns into a strong wall.
You recapture with the pawn and open the a-file for your rook later. Smart structure.
White lifts the rook to the e-file. No direct threat; time for you to start your own plan.
Too passive — your queen move does little. The strong plan was g5, pushing pawns at White's king. Lesson: when both sides are calm, be the one who attacks first.
White's king step is a real slip and loses time. Punish it now with g5, charging your pawns at his king.
Yes — g5 begins your pawn storm toward White's king. Great, you found the right plan.
White breaks in the center to open lines. Stay calm and keep pushing your attack.
Strong — g4 kicks White's knight and keeps your attack rolling. Well done.
White captures your e5 pawn. Take it back the right way to keep your attack alive.

Mistake — taking with the knight lets White trade and kill your attack. Take back with the pawn (dxe5) so your g4 pawn keeps White's knight in trouble. Lesson: in an attack, recapture in the way that keeps your threats going.
White grabs your knight. Just take back and the position stays roughly level.
Good — you recapture and keep your pawns solid. Fine move.
White pushes the h-pawn to challenge your pawn chain. Keep your pieces active.
Your bishop develops onto a long line, which is okay. (b5 was a hair sharper, but this is fine.)
White offers a bishop trade that slightly helps you. Take it with Bxd5 and you are happy.
Good — you accept the trade on great terms. Simple and correct.
White recaptures with the pawn. The game is still even, so keep playing carefully and stay active.
Your opponent plays e4, the most common first move. It grabs the center. Get ready to fight for the middle squares.
You played d5, hitting the center. The engine likes c5 a bit more, but this is fine and starts a real fight.
He takes your pawn with exd5. This is normal. Now take it back so you don't lose a pawn for nothing.
You took back with the queen, Qxd5. It works, but bringing the queen out early lets him gain time by chasing it. Nf6 first was a touch cleaner. Lesson: early queens get pushed around.
He played Nf3 to develop. Good for you — now you can pin his knight. Bg4 is the strong reply.
Bg4! The best move. Your bishop pins his knight to the queen and helps your plan. Nice and natural.
He blocks with Be2. Calm and safe. Keep developing — bring out your knight with Nc6.
You played Nf6 to develop the knight. Solid, though Nc6 was a shade better to grab the center fast. Still a good piece out.
He pushed c4, gaining space and nudging your queen. Just step the queen to safety — Qd7 keeps everything connected.
You retreated to Qd8. A little passive; Qd7 was better because it stays active and keeps your pieces talking. Lesson: retreat forward when you can, not all the way home.
He played Nc3 to develop. No threat to you. Continue your plan and put your last knight out with Nc6.
Nc6, finishing your development. Exactly right — all your minor pieces are doing a job now.
He played a3, a slow pawn move that wastes time. You can grab the moment to push e5 and take the center.
e5! The best move. You seize the center and free your pieces. Great use of his slow move.
He castled, getting his king safe. Normal. You keep building — your pieces are well placed.
You played Bc5, aiming the bishop at his king's side. Decent, but pushing e4 to kick his knight was stronger and more active.
He played b4 to push your bishop and gain space. Don't just retreat passively — Bd4, planting the bishop in the center, was strong.
You went Be7, all the way back. That gives up the active spot; Bd4 kept the bishop strong and annoying. Lesson: don't retreat a good piece without a reason.
He played Bb2, lining his bishop up on the long diagonal at your center. Watch that pawn on e5. Castle and stay solid.
You castled, O-O. Good and safe — king tucked away, rook ready to help. Best move here.
He played Re1, putting a rook on the open file. His pressure is growing on the center. Pushing e4 to gain space was the active answer.

Nd4 was a mistake — it loses material after trades. He just takes the knight and you come out worse. e4 was much better, gaining space safely. Lesson: before jumping a knight in, check what happens after he takes it.
He took with Nxd4, the right move. Now take back with the pawn, exd4, to keep things tidy.
You took with Qxd4. The pawn (exd4) was better because it keeps your structure and doesn't expose the queen. Now your queen can get chased again.
He played Na4 — this is a slip. You can win his light bishop's tempo with Bxe2, trading off and staying fine. Take the bishop.
Bxe2! Best move. You trade bishops and avoid trouble. Clean choice.
He took back with the rook, Rxe2, instead of the queen. That lets you grab his loose c4 pawn — Qxc4 wins it!
You played Qd7, missing the free pawn. Qxc4 just won material. Lesson: when something is hanging, check if you can take it before doing anything else.
He grabbed your e5 pawn with Bxe5. He's a pawn up now. Stay active — put a rook on the open file with Rfe8.
You played Ng4, jumping the knight toward his side. It's fine and pokes at his bishop. A rook to e8 was also good.
He played Bg3, retreating the bishop. This is loose — you can strike with f5, gaining space and rolling your pawns forward.
You played Bf6 instead. That missed the strong f5 push, which grabbed the moment. Bf6 is okay but less active. Lesson: pawn breaks like f5 can take over the game.
He played Rc1, lining up on the c-file. No direct threat. Solidify with b6 to keep his pieces out.
You played h5, pushing on the side. A bit slow; b6 was better to control squares and keep things firm. Side pawns can wait when the center matters.
He played Nc5, an active knight jump eyeing your pawns. Keep an eye on b7. Your queen should stay flexible.
You played Qd8. Fine move keeping the queen safe and connected. No real loss here.
He played Nxb7, snatching a pawn. Don't panic — chase the knight and stay active with Qc8.
Qc8! Best move. You hit the knight and keep your pieces working. Good response.
He played Nc5, hopping the knight back to safety. Calm position. Keep your pieces active and look for pawn pushes.
Bb2 was a mistake — the bishop drifts to a spot that doesn't help and loses value. Pushing h4 to gain space was much better. Lesson: keep pieces where they do real work.
He played Rb1, attacking your bishop on b2. You must move it — Bf6 brings it back to a useful diagonal.
You played Bxa3, grabbing a pawn. It wins a pawn but the bishop gets a bit stuck out there; Bf6 was steadier. Still, a pawn is a pawn.
He played Rb3, eyeing your bishop and the b-file. Your bishop is in some danger. The active try was h4, pushing your own attack.
You played a5 to support the bishop. Okay, but h4 kept your kingside pawns rolling and was stronger. Don't forget your own attack.
He took the bishop with Rxa3, the best move. You can't save it, so play on — h4 keeps your counterplay alive.
You took back with axb4, winning the pawn. Good — you keep material balanced after the trades.
He played Rb3 instead of trading rooks. A small slip. Bring your rook to a5 to stay active and pressure him.
You played Qb8, which is a bit awkward and lets him take over. Ra2, putting your rook on the active file, was better. Lesson: keep rooks active, not passive.
He played Nd7, forking your queen and rook area. You must save your queen — Qd8 keeps it safe and defends. Be careful, his knight is busy.
Great start. You play the king's pawn out two squares, the most popular first move. It grabs space in the middle right away.
Your opponent copies you and meets you in the center. Just keep developing your pieces — bring out a knight next.
Nice and natural. Your knight comes out and attacks the black pawn on e5. This is normal opening play.
Black defends the e5 pawn with the knight. Nothing scary — carry on getting your pieces out.
Good. Your bishop aims at the f7 square near the black king, a strong spot. This is the Italian Game setup.
Black pushes the f-pawn and weakens the king. This is a small mistake. The clean reply was d4 to open the center and use Black's loose position.
Taking the pawn looks tempting, but it lets Black get going. Better was d4, hitting the center hard. Lesson: grab the center before grabbing a small pawn.
Black develops the knight and keeps building. Stay calm and finish getting your king safe.
Castling makes your king safe, which is good. But d4 was stronger to fight for the middle. Lesson: in open games, central pawns come first.
Black's pawn pushes to e4 and pokes your knight. Just move the knight to safety, like the engine's Nh4.
You move the knight to g5, eyeing weak squares near Black. A fine spot for it.
Black plays d5 to gain space. Keep your pieces active and watch that f5 pawn you can win back.
You put your bishop on b5 to pin the knight. A solid idea, very close to best.
Black takes your f5 pawn back. That's fair — pieces are roughly even now, so just keep developing.
Bringing the knight out is okay, but d3 was better to free your other pieces and grab the e4 pawn later. Lesson: don't leave your back pieces stuck.
Black's bishop comes to c5 and points at your king's corner. Watch your f2 and king safety — play d3 to calm things down.
Excellent. d4 strikes the center and challenges Black's bishop. This is your best move here.
Black's bishop steps back to b6, still aiming at your king. Support your center with f3 like the engine wants.
Pushing the a-pawn is slow. Far better was f3 to break Black's strong e4 pawn. Lesson: deal with the enemy's strong pawn before side-pawn moves.
Black castles, but this drops a piece! Play Bxc6 right now — you win material because of the pin on the knight.
Black's knight jumps to g4 to hit your bishop. You can still play Bxc6 to win the knight on c6.
a5 attacks the bishop, but Bxc6 was still the strong winning move. Lesson: keep looking for that same idea until it's gone.
Good, you recapture and your pawns now cover key central squares. Simple and correct.
Black's queen grabs your g5 knight, but this is a mistake. Play axb6 — you take Black's bishop and stay ahead.
Black's bishop comes to h3 near your king. Keep calm — the engine likes Qe2 to stay solid.
Trading rooks on f8 is fine and keeps things simple. Roughly equal value.
Black takes back with the rook. Steady play continues — try Bf1 to deal with the bishop on h3.
Qd2 is okay but a little loose; Bf1 was cleaner to kick the h3 bishop. Near equal, so no big worry.
Black's queen takes your d5 knight — a mistake. Play Bxc6 to win Black's knight back and keep the balance in your favor.
Perfect. Bxc6 grabs the knight, your best move. You keep the material fair.
Black recaptures with the queen. Fine — now push your passed a-pawn with axb6 ideas.
You take on b6, making a dangerous passed pawn on the side. A reasonable plan.
Black's bishop goes to e6, but it lets your pawn run. Play bxa7 — your pawn is one step from queening.
Good, bxa7 pushes your pawn to the edge, almost a new queen. Strong and correct.
Black plays b6 to try and stop you, but it's slow. The push c4 keeps the pressure and opens lines.
Qb4 is active, but c4 was stronger to support your attack and that a7 pawn. Lesson: keep pushing your passed pawn with help.
Black brings the rook to a8 to round up your a7 pawn. Defend it and keep your queen busy — c4 was the idea.
b3 is too quiet and lets Black grab your c2 pawn. Better was Qe7 to make threats. Lesson: when ahead, stay active, don't sit back.
Black's queen snaps off your c2 pawn. Not a disaster — get active with Qe7 and keep your pieces working.
Good, Qe7 puts your queen on a strong square and makes threats. The best move here.
Black's queen retreats to c6 to guard. Keep pressing — the engine likes d5 to open things up.
You push b4 to roll your queenside pawns forward. A fine plan, basically best.
Black's bishop sits on d5 to block and defend. Stay patient and keep your pawns and queen pushing.
b5 walks into trouble; h4 was safer and kept your edge. Lesson: don't push a pawn if it leaves your king or pieces loose.
Black plays Qb7 instead of the strong Qc3, a mistake that helps you. Grab the center with Qe5 to take over.
You missed Qe5. Rc1 is okay but the strong central queen move was much better. Lesson: a queen in the middle does the most.
Black's Rc8 is a blunder! Play Qd7 — your queen jumps to a great square and your a7 pawn and threats take over.
Excellent, Qd7 is the strong move. Your queen now dominates and your passed pawn is a monster.
Black makes luft with h6 to give the king air. Keep your plan — bring the rook in and push pawns.
g3 is a bit slow; h3 was tidier. A small inaccuracy, nothing major.
Black's king steps to h7 for safety. Just keep improving — double up or push your g-pawn.
The check feels active but chases the king to a better spot; Rc2 to bring the rook in was stronger. Lesson: don't check just to check.
Black's king goes to h8 in the corner. Now bring more force over — your pieces aim at the king.
Qd7 is okay but Rc6 was stronger to crash in. Small slip, you're still winning big.
Black's Bg8 is a blunder. Play Rc6 — your rook swings over and the attack with your queen crushes Black.
You missed the win again. Rf1 is too passive; Rc6 was the killer. Lesson: when your rook can join the attack, use it.

They develop their knight to f6. A normal move; nothing to fear. Keep building your position.
Knight to f3 — good development. Tiny note: pushing the d-pawn to d4 was a touch better to grab more center, but this is fine.
They bring a knight to c6. A small slip by them. You can answer by playing d4 to take the big center.
You castle to safety. Solid. The engine slightly preferred d4 first, but a safe king is never wrong at your level.
They play a6, making a little room for their pieces. No threat. You should grab the center with d4.
b3 is a bit slow. Better was d4 to take the strong center — that pawn would give you more space and a clear plan. Lesson: in open positions, fight for the center first.
They push b5, gaining space on the side. It looks scary but it weakens their pawns. You still want to play d4 in the middle.
a3 is again too slow and lets your edge slip. d4 was the move — claim the center while you can. Lesson: don't drift on the sides; play in the middle.
They finally tuck the queen to d6, a good safe spot. Time for you to get active — strike with d4.
Good — d4 at last! Now you own the center and your pieces have room to work.
They play e6 to free their dark bishop. A normal, solid move. Just keep developing your pieces.
Bishop to g5 pins and pressures their knight. A reasonable plan, though simply Bd3 to aim at their king was a touch cleaner.
They block with the bishop on e7. Expected. Now connect your plan — bring your queen and rooks into the game.
Queen to d2 — lovely. It supports your g5 bishop and gets ready to swing toward their king.
They castle their king into safety on the kingside. Fine for them. Notice their king now lives near your g5 bishop — keep that in mind.
Rook to d1 puts a rook on the open file behind your queen. Good teamwork between your pieces.
They develop the bishop to b7 on the long line. Calm move. You can now take on f6 to damage the pawns near their king.
Bxf6 — great idea! You trade to wreck the pawns guarding their king. This opens the door to attack.
They take back with the g-pawn, but this badly breaks the shield around their king. This is a big blunder. Punish it now with Knight to e4, heading straight for the weak king.
Ne4 — exactly right. Your knight jumps toward their king and threatens to leap into f6 with crushing effect.
Their queen goes to d5 to defend. Good try by them, but your attack rolls on — bring the queen to h6 and pile in.
Qh6 — superb! Your queen joins the attack right next to their king. The threats are getting deadly.
They retreat the queen to d8 — a game-losing blunder; it stops guarding the kingside. Strike with Knight takes f6 check, winning the king's cover by force.
Nxf6+ — yes! A check that rips open the king and forces their reply. The attack is now winning.
They must capture your knight with the bishop. Forced. Keep the attack flowing.
Bishop to d3 — brilliant aim. Your bishop now points at h7 right next to their king, setting up the finish.
They play Re8, but it cannot stop your attack. Keep going.
Bxh7+ — a beautiful sacrifice with check! You tear the last cover off their king.
Their king hides on h8. Forced, and it walks into your mating net. Continue the chase.
Bg6+ — perfect. The bishop steps back with check and traps the king in the corner.
King back to g8, forced. The end is one step away — bring the queen in.
Qh7+ — the queen lands next to the king with check, driving it to its doom.
King to f8, the only square. Now finish it.
Qxf7# — checkmate! A clean finish. Lesson: when you break open the enemy king, throw your pieces at it fast — knight, bishop, and queen worked together perfectly. Well played!
You start with the king's pawn going to the middle. Great first move — it grabs the center and opens lines for your pieces.
You take the pawn. Perfect — simple and strong.
Black takes back with the queen too early. Good news for you: the queen is in the open and you can chase it to gain time.
Your knight jumps out and attacks the black queen. Nice — you develop a piece and make the queen move again.
The queen gives a check from e6. It looks scary but it just helps you: block it and keep developing.
You block the check with your bishop. Calm and correct.
Black brings out a knight. Normal developing move — keep getting your pieces out.
Your knight comes out. Fine. Pushing the d-pawn to d4 was a touch better to own the center.
Black develops a knight to c6. Just keep your plan and finish bringing pieces out.
You castle and tuck your king safe. Good habit. Playing d4 first was also strong.
Black moves the queen to d7. Quiet move — you can take the center with d4.
Knight to the edge on b5 — a mistake. Play d4 instead, because on the rim the knight does nothing and gets kicked. Lesson: keep knights near the center.
Black plays a6 and kicks your knight, just as expected. You have to retreat now.
You bring the knight back to c3. Best square — undo the earlier rim trip.
Knight to g5 — a small mistake. Re1 was better. The g5 knight can be chased by h6 and has no good target. Lesson: don't jump a knight where a pawn shoos it away.
Black plays b5 to gain space, but it weakens their setup. You can hit it with a4.
You play d3, but a4 was much better to attack the b5 pawn. Lesson: when the enemy pushes pawns on the side, strike at them fast.
Black puts a bishop on c5, aiming at your king side. Watch that bishop and meet it with your own pieces.
Your bishop goes to e3 to face the c5 bishop. Good — you offer a trade and stay solid.
Black's bishop steps to d4. You can simply swap it off.
You take the bishop on d4. Fine trade, fewer attackers near your king.
Black takes back with the pawn. Now you can re-route your knights to strong squares.
Knight to e4 — well done. It eyes great central squares.
Black trades knights on e4. Just take back and you keep a nice central knight.
You recapture with the knight. Strong piece in the middle — good job.
Black castles to safety. Both kings are tucked away; now make a plan in the center.
Knight to c5 is okay but Re1, using your rook, was a bit better. Lesson: put rooks on open files.
Black's queen steps to d5. No threat — keep improving your pieces.
Knight back to e4. Small step; Nb3 was a touch better. Still fine.
Black lifts a rook to b8. They are getting ready to push on the side — stay alert.
Bishop to f3 hits the long line and eyes black's queen side. Good move.
Black's queen comes to e5. You can grab the e-file with a rook and stay solid.
Queen to d2 connects your pieces. Reasonable; a rook to e1 was also good.
Black's rook swings to b6. They may attack on the side — keep your pieces ready.
Rook to e1 takes the open file. Nice — that is the right home for the rook.
Black plays h6 to make a little air for the king. No danger; carry on with your plan.
You play c3 — a mistake that opens lines near your own king. b4 was better to push on the side. Lesson: don't crack open your own king's shelter.
Black's queen swings to f5, eyeing your king. Get pieces back to defend and stay calm.
You play b4, but Ng3 to guard was better. Lesson: when the enemy queen aims at you, defend first.
Black plays Ne5 and attacks your bishop on f3 — a half-loose move you can answer. Save the bishop with Bd1 and you are fine.
Ng3 is a big blunder — it lets Black win your bishop with check. Bd1 saves the bishop instead. Lesson: when a piece is attacked, move it to safety before anything else.
Black takes your bishop with check on f3. Forced for you to take back now.
You recapture with the pawn. Correct — you had no choice, but your king is now very open.
Black's queen grabs the f3 pawn and gets close to your king. You must defend the mate squares right now.
Ne2 is a fatal slip — it allows a forced mate. Qe2 was needed to block and trade. Lesson: when the enemy queen is near your bare king, count the mate threats first.
Black plays Bb7, lining the bishop up for mate on the long line. The threat is mate next move and it is very hard to stop.
Nf4 does not stop the mate. The position was already lost after the open king.
Black plays Qh1 — checkmate. The whole finish came from the open king side; next game, keep your king covered and check for mate threats before you move.
You start with the king pawn going to e4. A strong, normal first move that opens lines for your pieces.
Black pushes d5 and offers a pawn trade in the center. This is the Scandinavian idea. Just take the pawn — it is safe for you.
You take on d5 and win the center pawn. Nice and simple.
Black takes back with the queen very early. This helps you: your next move can develop a piece and chase the queen with tempo.
Knight to c3 develops a piece AND attacks the black queen for free time. Great use of the early queen.
Black's queen runs back home to d8. You have gained time and a head start in development.
Bishop to c4 is okay but a bit early; Nf3 was better to develop your knight first. Lesson: get your knights and king safety going before fancy bishop spots.
Black plays g6 to put the bishop on the long line. A little slow — you should grab the center now with d4.
d4 builds a big strong center with two pawns. Exactly the right plan. Well done.
Black puts the bishop on g7, aiming at your center. Keep developing calmly with your knight and king safety.
Bishop to e3 develops and supports your d4 pawn. A solid, quiet move.
Black brings a knight to c6 to press your d4 pawn. Just keep developing; your center is fine.
Queen to f3 brings the lady out too soon; Nf3 was better. Lesson: develop knights and bishops first, not the queen.
Black develops the knight to f6, a normal good move. Nothing to fear yet — finish your development.

Castling queenside is a big mistake here. Black can play Bg4 to pin your queen, then win your rook with Bxd1; Nge2 was much safer. Lesson: don't castle into a spot where one move attacks your queen and rook.
As warned, Black's bishop jumps to g4 and attacks your queen. Move the queen to safety with Qf4.
Queen to f4 is the right move, getting out of the attack. Good save.
You recapture with Nxd1. The game goes on, just down a little material now.
Black's knight hops to d5 to bother your queen. Keep your bishop — move the queen to f3 instead of trading.
Taking the knight with Bxd5 gives away your good bishop; Qf3 was better, keeping the bishop. Lesson: don't trade a strong bishop unless you must.
Black takes back with the queen on d5. Now develop your last knight and try to get active.
Knight to f3 develops and is a fine, active move. Good.
Black castles instead of grabbing your a2 pawn — a slow choice that helps you. Play Nc3 to bring your knight out and chase the black queen.
Grabbing the c7 pawn with Qxc7 looks tempting but is a mistake; Nc3 was better. Lesson: don't go pawn-hunting with your queen when your own pieces still need to get active.
Black plays Rfc8 to attack your queen on c7. The strong reply is Nc3, developing with threats against the d5 knight.
Taking the b7 pawn with Qxb7 keeps the queen wandering and is again worse than Nc3. Lesson: one more pawn is not worth leaving your other pieces asleep.
Black takes your a2 pawn with Qxa2, a good and natural grab. Bring your knight to c3 to chase the queen and get your pieces working.
Your opponent played c3, a slow pawn move that does not fight for the middle. That gives you a free hand — take the center with e5.
Nice — e5 plants a pawn in the center and opens lines for your pieces.
d3 is passive and gives up the center fight. Push d5 now so you own both center squares.
Perfect — d5 builds a strong two-pawn center. You are already a little better here.
h3 is another slow move that does not develop. Just keep building: bring out a piece like Bd6 or the knight.
Bd6 develops your bishop to a good square aiming at the kingside. A fine, simple developing move.
Big mistake by your opponent — g4 throws a pawn forward and badly weakens the king's home. Punish it right away with h5, hitting the g4 pawn.
Good — h5 attacks the loose g4 pawn and questions his shaky kingside.
g5 pushes past instead of trading, leaving more holes near his king. Calmly develop with Be6 and aim at those weak squares.
This is the costly move of the game. f6 blocks your own pieces and opens lines near your king; far better was Be6 to develop the bishop and keep your big center solid.
h4 is another weak pawn push that ignores development. Grab the chance with Bg4 — your bishop comes out with tempo and pressure.
Qd7 is a bit slow and lets the edge get loose. Better was Na6 to bring the knight into play and prepare to castle.
Qb3 eyes your b7 pawn and the d5 pawn. Keep things safe and active with Qf7, guarding and unpinning.
Qc6 keeps your queen active and defends d5; a reasonable choice, though Qf7 was a touch tidier.
Bg2 is a good move — his bishop now stares at your d5 pawn. Answer by developing with Ne7 to add a defender.
Be6 leaves your knight and king stuck at home; Ne7 was better, getting a piece out and readying castling. Try to develop knights before moving the same pieces twice.
A blunder — Nd2 blocks his own bishop and wastes time when c4 was needed. Seize the moment with Nd7, improving your knight toward the strong c5 square.
Na6 heads for c5 but the rim is slow; Nd7 reached the same plan faster. Still, the idea of c5 is right.
a3 is a small, slow pawn move that does not threaten anything. Continue your plan with Ne7 to finish developing.
Nc5 is an active outpost for your knight, eyeing his queen and weak squares; Ne7 was a hair better but this is fine.
Qc2 is his best move, lining up on the c-file and defending. Stay calm and keep improving with Nd7 to bring your last knight to life.
You start with the classic king-pawn opening. Good first move that grabs the center.
Black answers with e6, the French Defense. This blocks the bishop in but is solid. Keep building your center with d4.
You play d4 and now own a strong two-pawn center. Exactly the right plan against this setup.
Black pushes d5 to challenge your center. This is normal in the French. You can keep tension or trade.
Black takes back with the pawn. The center is now open and symmetrical, so easy piece play is coming.
Bishop to f4 develops a piece, but Nf3 first was smoother. Small slip, your position is still healthy. Lesson: get knights out early before the bishops.
Black develops the knight to f6, eyeing the center. Just keep developing too, like Bd3.
Knight to c3 brings out another piece. Bishop to d3 was a hair better, but this is totally fine.
Black pins your knight with Bb4. It is annoying but not scary. You can break the pin later with a3.
Knight to e2 is a bit passive and lets the pin off awkwardly. Bishop to d3 was better to finish developing fast. Lesson: put pieces on their best square, not just a safe one.
Black castles and is now safe. You should kick the bishop with a3 soon.
You play a3 to ask the bishop a question. Good idea, now it must retreat or trade.
Black trades the bishop for your knight with check. This actually helps you a little — you get the two bishops. Just recapture with Nxc3.
You take back with the knight. Perfect, now you have both bishops, a small long-term plus.
Bishop to e2 blocks the check and develops. Clean and correct.
Black plays Bg4 to pin, but this is a mistake. Punish it with f3! After f3 the bishop must move and your bishop on f4 can grab the c7 pawn. Lesson: a pin can be chased away by a pawn.
You play f3 and kick the bishop. Strong move that wins time.
Black retreats the bishop to h5, keeping a loose pin on f3. You can develop with Qd2 and prepare to castle long or push g4.
You castle kingside to get safe. Solid, though Qd2 first was a touch sharper. Your king is fine now.
Black plays a6, a slow move. Use the free time to improve a piece, like a rook to e1.
Black develops the knight to c6, pressing your d4 pawn. Just support it and keep your pieces active.
You push g4 to gain space and chase the h5 bishop. A bit risky near your king, but playable.
Black retreats the bishop to g6, offering a trade. Trading is fine for you.
You take the bishop on g6. Good, this opens the h-file a little and trades off his active piece.
Black recaptures with the pawn. The position is calm; now build a plan with your queen and rooks.
Rook to f2 lifts the rook for defense and doubling later. A small idea, position stays equal.
Black's knight goes to h7, a passive spot. You have a free moment — centralize with Qd2 or Qd3.
Queen to d2 connects your rooks and eyes the kingside. Right square for the queen.
Black pushes g5 to grab space. Don't panic — your bishop can slide to g3 and stay strong.
Bishop to e3 is fine, but Bg3 kept it on a better diagonal. Very minor, nothing lost.
Black's knight jumps to a5, heading for c4. Meet it calmly — b3 stops the knight from landing on c4.

This is a big mistake. f4 drops material because after Nc4 your queen and bishop get forked and you lose the bishop on e3. Better was b3 to block the knight first. Lesson: before pushing pawns, check if it opens your own pieces to attack.
Black plays Nc4 and wins your bishop, just as the trouble showed. From here, save what you can — try fxg5 to grab a pawn back and keep fighting.
White opens with the king pawn. Just bring out your pieces and stay calm.
You played d5 in the middle, but c5 was better. The problem is d5 lets White push past and grab space. Lesson: against the king pawn, c5 fights for the center more safely.
White pushed the pawn past instead of taking yours, which actually helps you. Hit back by pushing your pawn to d4 to take space.
Good idea — you put your bishop outside the pawns where it is active. This is the right way to develop this bishop.
White builds a big pawn center. Keep developing and plan a pawn break later.
Solid move: it supports your d-pawn and opens a path for your dark bishop.
White grabs space with f4 but weakens his own position. Strike the center now with c5.
You developed your knight, but c5 was stronger to hit White's center right away. The center is getting big and needs to be challenged. Lesson: break a big center with a pawn before it gets strong.
White develops his knight. Nothing scary; continue your plan.
Nice jump — your knight attacks White's bishop and squares near his king. This is the engine's top choice.
White put his bishop where your knight can take it. Grab it: Nxd3+ wins the bishop with check.
Perfect — you take the bishop with check and win the bishop pair.
White takes back but now has doubled, weak pawns. These pawns are a target for you.
You bring the knight out, heading to f5. The tiny improvement was c6 first, but this is fine.
White gives a check that just wastes time. Simply block with c6 and you stand well.
Good — you block the check with a solid pawn and keep your position strong.
White's queen goes back, having lost time. You are comfortable; keep developing.
Your queen eyes White's weak pawns. Bg4 was a touch more active, but this is okay.
White castles to safety. Now finish getting your own king safe.
You develop the bishop, but Bg4 was more active because it goes after the knight. Both your moves were a bit passive. Lesson: put bishops where they make threats.
White develops his last knight. Nothing to fear; finish developing.
Castling keeps your king safe, which is good, but the active Bg4 was even better. When you are doing well, keep up the pressure. Lesson: stay active even after castling.
White's knight attacks your queen but goes to the edge. Play Qb5 to keep your queen active and safe.
Great — your queen steps back safely and now aims at White's weak d3 pawn.
White's knight attacks your queen and bishop at once. Just take it with your bishop.
Correct — you take the knight and remove the threat.
White takes back. His pawns are still weak and ready to be attacked.
Well done — your bishop finally grabs the weak d3 pawn, so you win a pawn.
White's rook goes to a passive spot. You are better; use your extra pawn.
Your knight jumps in actively. The quiet b6 to hit the c5 pawn was also good, but this is fine.
White's rook attacks your bishop on d3. Keep your bishop and knight safe.

This knight jump looks scary but it loses a lot of value; Be4, keeping everything solid, was much better. You got lucky that White did not punish it. Lesson: before a fancy jump, check that your piece won't get into trouble.
White's queen attacks your knight and the b7 pawn. Find a move that saves the knight and stays active.
Clever — your knight forks White's rook in the corner. This is the best move.
White grabbed a pawn but left his rook in the corner. Take it: Nxa1 wins the whole rook.
Yes — you take the rook in the corner and win big material.
White's queen comes to hit your corner knight. Keep your queen active and don't panic.
Good — you grab another pawn and your queen stays very active.
White puts his knight in the center. Stay alert, but you are still winning.
Your queen drifts to the side; Qc4 was better to offer a trade while you are ahead. Trading helps the side with more material. Lesson: when ahead, swapping pieces makes winning easier.
White's pawn attacks your queen and tries to trap your corner knight. Be careful with that knight.
Better was Nxb3 to free your trapped corner knight. As played, the knight stays stuck in the corner. Lesson: a trapped piece is worth saving, even by giving a little material back.
White wastes a move. Play b6 to break up his c5 pawn and open lines.
You try to run the corner knight out, but it just gets captured; b6 was much better. The c2 square was guarded. Lesson: check if a square is protected before you move there.
White takes your knight, so you lost that piece. Play simply now and use your remaining pieces.
Your queen repositions safely. The pawn move a5 was a small improvement, but this is okay.
White pushes a pawn and overextends. Centralize with Qc4 to grab the initiative.
You try to break White's center, but Qc4 was stronger and more active. Lesson: an active queen in the center is powerful.
White did not take your f-pawn. Look to open the position in your favor with Qc4.
Taking here lets White's queen jump into the center. Qc4 first was better. Lesson: opening lines can also help your opponent — check who really benefits.
White's queen takes and sits strong in the center. Watch its threats and defend carefully.
You bring a rook to the open file, which is okay. Qc4 was a bit more active.
White's bishop aims at the long line toward your king. Keep an eye on that diagonal.
Good — your rook guards your second rank. This is basically the best move.
White pushes f5 and weakens himself. Hit back with Qc4 to attack.
Both rooks went passive; Qc4 was far more active. When you can attack, don't curl up. Lesson: in a good spot, keep making threats instead of retreating.
Big mistake by White. Take the pawn with exf5 and you are right back in the game.
Taking with the pawn (exf5) was safer and kept your structure; the rook capture lets White's queen jump to d6. Lesson: a pawn is often the safest piece to capture with.
White's queen pushes deep into your camp. This is dangerous; defend and keep your king safe.
Walking your king into the open is risky; Ref7, joining your rooks, was safer. Now your king is exposed. Lesson: in danger, bring defenders together, don't expose your king.
White's knight attacks your rook on f5. Move it to safety.
You save your rook — this is the best move in a tough spot.
White checks your king. The engine says trade with Qxf1+ to calm things down.
Walking the king up runs into trouble and loses your rook; Qxf1+ to trade was the way to fight on. Lesson: when checked in danger, trading pieces is often the safest choice.
White takes your rook and is now winning. A tough finish — but you played many strong moves earlier, especially winning that rook in the corner.
Your opponent opens with the most common first move, grabbing the center. Just develop your pieces and stay calm.
You answer in the center — this is the Scandinavian Defense idea. A move like c5 was a touch better, but this is fine for your level.
They take your pawn. No worry — you can win it back next move.
You grab the pawn back with your queen. Careful: the queen sits in the open and will get chased around.
Their knight jumps out and attacks your queen. You must move her to safety.
You slide the queen to a5, a normal and safe square in this opening. Good choice.
They develop a knight. Notice you could pin it with your bishop later.
You bring out your knight and develop. Solid and natural.
They take the full center with a pawn. Nothing to fear yet — keep developing.
You pin their knight to the queen with your bishop. Nice active idea.
They poke your bishop with a pawn. Taking the knight here (Bxf3) is clean and simple.
You keep the pin by sliding back to h5. But this lets them push you around — trading on f3 was simpler.
They push the pawn to chase your bishop. Just step it back to g6.
You retreat the bishop. Fine — it stays on a safe diagonal.
Their knight jumps to a strong central square and eyes your bishop. Be ready to challenge it.
This knight jump is a mistake (better was Nbd7, bringing a piece out to help). Why: the knight on e4 gets kicked and you lose time.
They attack your knight with the queen. You have to move it again — wasted moves.
You tuck the knight back to d6. Okay, it is safe now.
They take your bishop, but this is a slip on their part. Just take back with the h-pawn (hxg6) and you are doing well.
You recapture and open the h-file for your rook. Good.
A quiet developing move. A good plan for you now is e6 to free your pieces.
Your queen eyes the b-pawn, but e6 was better to open lines for your pieces. Not a big error.
They push the pawn to cramp you. Bring your knight to d7 to get organized.
You develop the knight toward better squares. Good, sensible move.
They castle their king to safety on the queenside.
You castle too. Your king is now tucked away — well done.
Their bishop attacks your queen. A good answer is c5, fighting back in the center.
You move the queen to safety, but c5 gave you more active play. A small inaccuracy.
They drop their bishop's guard — a mistake. Punish it with g5! The pawn attacks the bishop and wins you material.
You missed the strong g5 here. Why g5 was better: it hits their bishop and wins time, while this quiet knight move lets them off the hook.
They swing the rook across to the center. Stay alert for a pawn break.
You pull the knight back, but the e5 break was strong here, hitting back in the center.
Their rook attacks your queen on a5. Move her to a safe spot.
You slide the queen to b6. Good — she is safe and active.
Big mistake by them — they offer a queen trade on a bad square. Take it with check: Qxe3+ wins material!
You take the queen with check. Excellent — you win the trade.
They take your queen back. The dust settles and you are doing fine.
A small move to make your king a bit safer. Okay.
They develop their bishop to the long diagonal.
You open the center with e6, but Nb6 was a bit better. Why: this opens lines that help their bishop too.
They take your pawn. Just take back.
You recapture with the f-pawn. Good, the center is even.
They offer a knight trade on e4. The simple answer is to take it: Nxe4.
This is a mistake — you should have taken the knight with Nxe4. Why: now their knight jumps to g5 and attacks your weak e6 pawn.
Their knight jumps in and hits your e6 pawn, just as warned.
You move the knight to c5, but Nd6 was steadier to guard your pawn. A small slip.
They take your knight. Take back.
You recapture with the bishop. Fine.
They jump the knight to fork your rooks, but it's a mistake! Grab the pawn first with Bxf2 — you come out ahead.
You missed the in-between Bxf2. Why: taking that pawn with the bishop first wins material before dealing with the fork.
Their knight takes your rook. Take it back.
You recapture the knight. The position has simplified.
A slow rook move by them. A good square for your knight now is d6.
You send the knight to d4, but Nd6 was better — it heads to stronger central squares.
Their king attacks your knight. The strong reply is the e5 pawn push.
You give a check with Nf3+, but the e5 push was better. Why: the check just makes their king step to a good square.
Their king steps aside. No harm done.
You park the knight on d2, but Nh4 was better — it stays active and grabs a pawn.
They attack your knight with the rook. A nice reply is to grab the f2 pawn with Bxf2.
You snatch the f2 pawn with the bishop. Good, you win a pawn.
Their rook gets active. Your knight to c4 was the strong move here.
You play Bc5, but Nc4 was better, hitting their rook with tempo. Small inaccuracy.
They offer a rook trade. Trading is fine.
You trade rooks. The endgame is simpler now.
They take back with the pawn.
Your bishop comes to e3, blocking and pinning. Good.
They take your knight with the rook — but the bishop can take it back. A clever idea is g5 first.
You take the rook back with check. Fine, though pushing g5 first was a touch stronger.
They take your bishop. Now it's a pawn endgame with bishops — stay active.
You walk your king up, but pushing your passed pawn with g5 was faster. Small slip.
They grab your b-pawn. Keep racing your own passed pawn.
You push your passed pawn forward. Good — this is your winning chance.
Their king marches over. Keep pushing and use your king.
You push the c-pawn. Okay, but watch your timing in the race.
Their bishop repositions. Use your king to support your pawns.
You centralize your king. Good — the king is a strong piece in the endgame.
They offer a pawn trade. Take it with check.
You take with check. Good.
They recapture. The race is on.
Your king steps to the center to attack their pawns. Strong.
Their king stays active too. Keep going for their pawns.
You head toward their kingside pawns. Good plan.
They take your c-pawn. Now push your own passed pawn fast.
You push the e-pawn forward. Great — this passer is your hope.
They push their own passed pawn. It's a pawn race now.
You go grab the kingside pawns with your king. Good idea.
They keep pushing their passer. Watch the race carefully.
You grab their h-pawn. Good, your king is eating pawns.
They move the bishop poorly — a mistake. Just keep grabbing pawns with Kxg4.
You take the g-pawn. Good, you keep collecting material.
They race their pawn forward. You should rush your own pawn with g5.
You bring the king back, almost as good as pushing. Fine.

d5! Finally the big central break. This opens the position while you are better developed. Lesson: when the center is open and your pieces are ready, strike.

dxe4 grabs a pawn and opens the center. Strong and clean.

dxe4 wins the pawn back. The material is even again; the game is roughly equal.
Castling long puts your king on the queenside, but g6 first was simpler. Your king is a little airy here, so play carefully.

Nf3 finally develops a knight. Nothing scary — continue your knight trip to g6.
Ng6 heads for the great f4 square. Good follow-up to your plan.
O-O puts your opponent's king in the corner — but it walked into your plan. The f4 jump is now very strong, so go Nf4.
Nf4 lands your knight on a powerful square near their king. Active and good.
Re1 is a calm rook move. Just keep improving — a bishop to e7 was tidy.
c4 pushes a pawn but loosens things. Be7 first, finishing development, was cleaner. Don't rush pawn moves before your pieces are out.

Bc5 develops your bishop with an eye on f2. Nice and active.
Rf1 defends the f2 spot. Keep the pressure; Nf4 was the clean way to keep squeezing.
Nxf2 sacrifices your knight, but it does not work here — you just lose material. Nf4 kept all your good pieces. Lesson: only sacrifice when you can clearly see it wins.
Rxf2 takes your knight. Now you are down a piece, so play for tricks and stay calm.
Bxf2+ wins one pawn back but trades off your strong bishop. h5 was steadier. After this you are still behind.
Qxf2 recaptures. Your opponent is up material now; look for active rook play to make it hard for them.
Rd3 is loose and lets a pawn fall. g5, gaining space, kept things tougher. Try to keep your pieces safe when behind.
Qxa7 grabs your a-pawn. Annoying, but your rook is active — Rhd8 brings your other rook into the game.
Kc7 walks the king out, but Rhd8 (developing the rook) was better. Your king is a bit exposed in the open.
Qc5+ gives a check but lets the queen be pushed back. Just step away with Kb8 and you're fine.

Nxc4 takes your pawn. You can take the knight back — Bxc4 keeps it simple.

Nxe5 recaptures. Defend carefully; activate your rooks and watch the passed pawns.
Re3 puts your rook on an active line. Good — active rooks are your best hope in the endgame.

b4 pushes a pawn forward. Watch the passed pawns, but you can win the a-pawn.

Rf3 is a slip that wastes time. Bring your rook back with Re7 to stay coordinated.

h4 starts pushing the h-pawn — that is the dangerous passed pawn. Double your rooks with Rce2 to stop it and attack.
b6 makes luft and supports your pawns, but doubling rooks (Rce2) was stronger. Keep an eye on that h-pawn.

Rxc3 wins a pawn back. Good — keep grabbing and stay active.
Nd2 covers and blocks. No threat; push your own passed pawns and stay busy.

g3 is slow and lets you get organized. Bring your other rook down with Rb2 for a strong setup.

Kb8 is fine, though Kc8 kept the king a touch more active. Not a real mistake.
Rd7 lines the rook up on the d-file. Keep your rooks active and push your passed b-pawn.
Rcc2 doubles your rooks on the second rank again. Great — this is the dream setup in rook endings.
h5 pushes the passed pawn, but it lets you crash in. Trade rooks with Rxd2+ and your own pawn races home.
Rxd2+ trades a pair of rooks with check. Strong — simplifying when you have a fast passed pawn is good.
Rxd2 recaptures, but this is losing for your opponent — your rook and b-pawn are too fast. Take the rook: Rxd2+ and push the pawn.
Rxd2+ trades the last rooks with check. Now it's a king-and-pawn race and your b-pawn is flying.

g4 pushes their pawns up the board. It's a race now — push your b-pawn and don't waste moves.
b5 starts your passed pawn rolling. Good — but bringing the king with Kc7 was even quicker.
g5 keeps their pawns running. Keep pushing b — count the moves so your pawn queens first.
Kc7 loses precious time in a race. Pushing b4 right away was needed; their pawns got dangerous. Lesson: in a pawn race, every single move counts — push, don't shuffle.
g6 races their pawn forward and now it's very close. You must push your b-pawn fast and watch for their queen.
Rg8 tries to stop the pawn, but your king belonged in front (Kd6). The race got scary. Use your rook and king together to stop their runners.
Kh4 marches their king up to help the pawns. Keep pushing b and keep your rook ready to block.
b4 pushes your passed pawn — the right idea. Keep it rolling toward queening.
Kg5 brings their king closer to shepherd their pawns. Push on with b3.
b3 keeps your pawn racing. Good — it's almost home.
h6 pushes their second runner. Both sides are close; push b2 and get ready to queen.
b2 — one step from a new queen! Keep going.
h7 means their pawn is also one step from queening. It's a photo finish; you must queen and give checks.
Rxg6+ is a big blunder — it throws away your rook and the win. Re8, stopping the h-pawn, kept you winning. Lesson: don't give up a rook unless it clearly wins on the spot.
Kxg6 takes your rook. Now you only have the pawn — promote it and try to give checks.
b1=Q+ makes a new queen with check! Good — now hunt their king with checks.
Kg7 steps away from the check. Keep checking and try to win their h-pawn or trap the king.
Qb2+ keeps checking. Fine — but try to line up checks that also stop their h-pawn from queening.
Kg8 hides near the corner. Keep giving safe checks and look for a way to grab the h7 pawn.
Qg2+ checks again. Good — keep the king busy so the h-pawn can't promote.
Kf7 steps out. Keep checking with care; their h-pawn is the only danger left.
Qh3 aims at the h-pawn — a good idea, though a check first kept the king pinned down. Try to win that pawn safely.
Kg7 guards the h-pawn. Keep maneuvering your queen to win it or force the king away.
Qg4+ checks again. Keep the checks coming while you circle the h-pawn.
Kf7 steps aside. Stay patient — line up a check that also attacks h7.
Qf5+ checks. Good — keep driving the king while watching the h-pawn.
Kg7 returns to defend. Keep the pressure; you want a check that wins the pawn.
Qe5+ checks the king. Patient queen work — keep going.
Kg8 hides in the corner. Keep checking and aim to capture h7.
Qe6+ checks again. Keep maneuvering closer to the h-pawn.
Kf8 steps out. Keep your checks safe and circle the pawn.
Qf6+ checks. Good — keep the king on the run.
Kg8 goes back to the corner. Stay patient and look to win h7.
Qg6+ checks again. You're slowly squeezing the king toward the edge.
Kh8 is forced into the corner. Now bring your king up (Kd8) to help finish the job.
Qe6 repositions the queen, but bringing your king with Kd8 was the real winning plan. Lesson: with a lone queen you often need your king's help to win.
Kg7 steps out of the corner. Keep checking, but remember to march your king up too.
Qe7+ checks. Useful, but don't forget to walk your king toward the action.
Kg8 hides again. Keep checks coming and start advancing your king.
Qe8+ checks. Fine — now bring the king closer each turn.
Kg7 steps out. Keep the king pinned and march your own king up.
Qe5+ checks again. Good control — add your king to the attack.
Kg8 retreats. Keep circling and bring the king forward.
Qe6+ checks. Patient play — your king should be marching now.
Kg7 steps out. Stay calm and keep improving your king.
Qg4+ checks. Keep the king boxed in while your king walks up.
Kh8 is forced into the corner. Use this moment to bring your king closer.
Qh5 eyes the h-pawn, but a check (Qc8+) kept the king trapped. Keep your queen active and helping.
Kg8 steps out. Keep checking and advancing your king together.
Qg6+ checks the king. Good — drive it back toward the corner.
Kh8 is pushed into the corner again. Bring your king up to deliver mate.
Qf6+ checks. Keep the king cornered while your king arrives.
Kg8 steps out once more. Stay patient; the win is just bringing your king up and checking together.
You start with the king pawn in the middle. This is a great first move and opens lines for your pieces.
