They push a4 to chase your bishop again. Keep it safe one more step.
Your bishop slides to a2, still active on the long line. Best move.
They line a rook up on the c-file against your bishop. Stay alert to that pin on c3.
The queen jump to e5 lets them get tricky with Rxc3. Better was Qb7, keeping everything safe and defended.
They miss their chance and play Nc6 instead. Now you can grab a free pawn with Qxb5.
Qg3 misses it. You should have taken the pawn with Qxb5 — it was just hanging there for free.
They push d5 in the center. Stay calm and find an active square for your knight.
Re1 is slow here. The strong move was Ne5, planting your knight in a powerful central spot.
Blunder by them with Na5. Punish it right away with Bxd5, winning the pawn and getting a great bishop.
You take the d5 pawn. Perfect — the best move and you grab material.
They lift a rook to a6. Just keep your pieces active.
Your bishop shifts to b4. A fine move, very close to the engine's choice.
They reroute the queen to d7. Stay focused and keep your pieces working.
Big blunder! Bd6 puts your bishop where it can simply be taken. Better was Be4, keeping the bishop safe and strong. Lesson: before moving, check if the square is defended.
They take your bishop for free with the rook. You lost that piece — keep playing carefully.
Ne5 is okay but Be4 was better, putting the bishop on a strong central line.
They put the queen on e7. A quiet move; keep improving your pieces.
Nxf7 gives the knight away for nothing — they just take with Rxd5. The calm Bf3 was much better. Lesson: don't sacrifice unless you see a clear payoff.
Your knight gives a check. It's fine, though Ne5 was a touch better.
Their king must step to h8. Forced, as expected.
Your knight comes back to g4 to stay safe. A reasonable move.
They grab your d4 pawn with the rook. Keep your pieces guarded.
Qe5 leaves your knight hanging — they win it with Rxg4. Better was Ne5 to keep the knight safe and active.
They take your knight for free. Tough loss; stay calm and grab pawns where you can.
You take the b5 pawn back to win some material. A good, solid move to fight on.

You start with the king pawn going two steps. This is the best and most popular first move — it grabs the center and frees your pieces. Lesson: opening the center early helps your pieces come out fast.
Your opponent copies you and meets you head-on, so now both sides fight for the middle. Nothing to fear here.
You bring out your knight and attack the black pawn in the center. Good, normal development.
Black defends the pawn with a knight. This is all very standard — keep developing.

You put your bishop on its best diagonal, aiming at the weak f7 square near the black king. This is the Italian Game, a great opening for you. Lesson: bishops love long open diagonals pointing at the enemy king.
Black brings out the other knight and pokes your center pawn. This is a known line; you have many good answers.
You push in the center to open lines. This is fine, but the quiet Ng5 was a touch sharper here.
Black takes your pawn. You can win it back; just recapture in good order.
You take back with the knight, but castling first was safer. After Nxd4 Black can grab your e-pawn with Nxe4. Lesson: when a recapture can wait, finish getting your king safe first.
Black grabs your center pawn with the knight, just as feared. The pawn count is even but his knight is loose in the middle.
You trade knights. It works, but the sharp Bxf7+ first was even stronger, hitting the king. Lesson: look for checks that hit the king before quiet trades.
Big mistake by Black! His queen comes out but leaves his pieces loose. Punish it with Qd4 — your queen guards your knight and stays in control with extra material.
You move the queen, but Qd4 was much better — it would have kept your knight safe and held your edge. Lesson: when ahead, protect the piece that is hanging first.
Another slip by Black — he takes with the pawn and forgets his knight on e4. It is now undefended: grab it with check by Qxe4+!
Perfect! You take the free knight with check and win a clean piece. This is the best move on the board. Lesson: a capture that also gives check is often winning.
Black blocks the check with his bishop. The danger is over; you are up a piece.
You step the queen back. The active Qf4 was a bit better, but you are still clearly ahead.
Black tucks his king away by castling. Sensible by him; keep building your own setup.
You castle and get your king safe. Smart and simple.
Black puts a rook on the half-open file to make some noise. Stay calm — your extra piece is what matters.
You support your center with a small pawn move. The active Qc3 was a bit stronger here, but this is okay.
Black pushes a pawn to gain space and poke your bishop. Just move the bishop to safety.
You drop the bishop back to a safe and strong square. Exactly right — 0 loss.
Black swings his bishop out. A touch loose; Bd6 was better for him. You are fine.
You reroute the bishop to aim toward the black king. Good, accurate move.
Black makes a small home for his king with the pawn. Harmless; keep improving your pieces.

This loses material. Pushing b4 opens the long dark diagonal straight to your rook in the corner. After Bxb4 cxb4 Black plays Qxa1 and wins your rook. Nd2 was safe. Lesson: before a pawn move, check what diagonals or lines it opens toward your own pieces.
Black takes the pawn, opening that fatal diagonal. You must recapture, but the rook in the corner is now in danger.
You recapture, but this opens the road to your corner rook. Sadly there was no good way out after b4.
Black's queen swings all the way down and takes your rook. You have lost the exchange; now play tight and use your remaining pieces.
You attack with the queen, but Nc3 was better — it develops and limits Black's queen. Lesson: develop a sleeping piece while making a threat.
Black's queen steps out to a central square. No immediate danger; keep your pieces working together.
You make a small pawn move to hold your queenside. Fine and safe.
Black centralizes the queen again. Just keep your pieces coordinated.
You develop the bishop and bump the queen. This is close to best, nothing to worry about.
Black drifts with the queen to the side; this was a little loose for him. Keep playing solid moves.
You put the rook on the half-open file. A reasonable, active move.
Black develops his bishop. You can simply trade it off if you like.
You trade bishops. It is fine, though keeping the queen active with Qc3 was a hair better.
Black takes back with the queen. Even trade; play on.
You plant the queen on the strong long diagonal. Excellent — best move, and it eyes Black's weak pawns.
Black makes a pawn move to cover squares. Now you can collect a loose pawn.
You snap up the c6 pawn for free. Nicely done — you win back material.
Black defends his back rows with the rook. A bit passive for him; keep pressing.
You finally bring your last knight into the game. Good — every piece should join in.
Black's queen sneaks in behind your lines. Watch your loose pieces; meet the queen head-on.

This is too passive and lets Black push d4 to attack your knight. Re2 was much better, kicking the queen and staying active. Lesson: don't hide a piece in the corner when you can challenge the enemy queen instead.
Black pushes the pawn and attacks your knight. You need to deal with this threat carefully.
This drops the knight. After Qc4 Black just plays dxc3 and wins it. Qe4 first was the saving move. Lesson: when a piece is attacked, defend or move it before making other plans.
Black takes your knight with the pawn. You can win the pawn back, but you have lost a piece here.
You recapture with the bishop, getting back onto the strong diagonal. Best move; make the most of what you have.
Black brings the queen over; this wandered a bit, Rd8 was better for him. Stay solid.
A loose pawn move that weakens your king a little. Bd4, centralizing the bishop, was stronger. Lesson: avoid pawn moves near your king unless you must.
Black tidies up his king. Quiet move; keep your rook and bishop active.
You bring the rook to the center where it is active. Good move.
Black pushes a pawn, but this loses it — take it with bxa5! Free pawn for you.
You swing the rook to attack instead. Also fine, but bxa5 simply winning the pawn was clean.
Black's queen shuffles back. No threat; keep an eye on grabbing that a-pawn.
You center the rook. Reasonable, though bxa5 winning the pawn was still on offer.
Black offers a queen trade. Since you are fighting to simplify, this is interesting for you.
You dodge the trade, but Qxb5 was the move — trading queens makes the game much easier. Lesson: when the position is even or you want calm, trading queens removes the danger.
Black activates his rook. He stands okay here; play steady.
You shift the queen; Qg4 was a touch more active. Minor.
Black moves the queen back again. Keep looking at the loose a-pawn you can win.
This misses the free a-pawn — bxa5 was clearly better and just wins it. Lesson: don't forget about easy pawns you can grab while you maneuver.
Black doubles his rooks on the open file to build pressure. Watch your back rank and meet him with Qf3 to stay active.
White opens with the king pawn. You answer with the Sicilian, a strong fighting setup for black.
You play c5, the Sicilian. This grabs space on one side and is a great pick. Lesson: meeting e4 with c5 gives you an active game.
White puts the bishop out early to c4. This is a bit loose. You can just keep building; develop your knight and pawns calmly.
You play e6 to make room for your pieces. Fine, though Nf6 (developing a knight with a hit) was a touch sharper.
White brings out a knight to c3. Nothing scary. Keep developing and aim to challenge the center.
You develop the knight to f6. Good and natural, but a6 (gaining queenside space) was the top choice here.
White plays a quiet pawn to d3. This is passive. You should strike in the center now while you can.
You play d5, hitting the center hard. This is the best move and frees your game nicely. Lesson: push d5 to grab the middle when white plays slow.
White trades pawns with exd5. Just take back so your center stays solid.
You recaptured with the knight, but taking with the pawn (exd5) was clearly better. The pawn keeps a strong center; the knight on d5 can get chased.
White jumps the knight to e4. This is a slip by white. You can grab the lead by playing Qc7, lining up your queen and keeping things tight.
You play a6 to stop white pieces from landing on b5. Solid, though Nc6 (quick development) was a bit better.
White develops the knight to f3. Normal. Just keep getting your pieces out and think about castling.
You play b5, gaining space on the queenside. This is the best move and pushes the white bishop back. Lesson: b5 grabs room and bothers the c4 bishop.
White retreats the bishop to b3. Expected. Now finish developing with your dark bishop and get the king safe.
Playing a5 weakens your pawns and lets white hit you with c4. Better was Be7 to develop and castle. Lesson: get your king safe before pushing more pawns.
White plays a4 to attack your b5 pawn. You need to deal with this; pushing b4 keeps your pawns strong and chases the knight.
Bd7 was a costly move; after axb5 your pawns crumble. Much better was b4, keeping the chain and gaining space. Lesson: when a pawn is attacked, push or defend it, don't ignore it.
White castled but missed axb5, which would have won material. You should grab the chance now: bxa4 wins back a pawn and frees you.
White plays c4 but again skips the winning axb5. Take with bxc4 right away to grab the pawn and ease your cramped position.
White takes your knight with the bishop. Simply take back with Qxf4 to keep the piece count even.
Your opponent opens with the queen pawn. This is a calm start. Just build your pieces in the middle too.
You answer in the center with d5. Nice and solid — you stake your own claim in the middle.
White brings out a knight, but it blocks his own c-pawn a little. Nothing to fear — keep developing.

Your knight to c6 also blocks your c-pawn. A small slip — Nf6 was tidier because it helps guard your center and gets ready to castle. Lesson: in these openings, the f6 square is usually the best home for this knight.
White develops his other knight. Calm move. Keep getting your pieces out.
You pin the knight with your bishop on g4. Good idea — Bf5 was a touch more active, but this is totally fine and natural.
White makes room for his bishop. No threat here — just continue your plan.
You push e5 to grab the center. This is the engine's top choice — well done, you are fighting for space.
White trades pawns in the middle. Simple — just take back and stay equal.
You recapture with the knight. Best move — your knight sits proud in the center.
White develops his bishop and offers a swap. Fine for you — you can choose how to trade.
You check and trade knights. This is fine, very close to equal, so no worries about it.
White takes back with the bishop, as expected. Now finish developing your pieces.
White grabs the loose d5 pawn. You can win that piece right back — just recapture.
You take the bishop back. Best move — you stay only one pawn down, not a piece.
White's knight jumps to d5, a strong central square. Try to kick it or trade it off soon.

Bishop to d6 develops, but the knight on d5 is still annoying. Nf6 was stronger because it challenges that knight and dares White to trade. Lesson: when an enemy piece is strong in your center, look for a move that attacks it.
White castles, but this lets you fight back. Play c6 right away to chase that knight off d5.
You play Nf6 to hit the knight. Good plan — though c6 first would have pushed it without offering a trade.
White takes your knight with check. Normal — just recapture and your queen gets active.
You take back with the queen. Best move — your queen now eyes White's position.
White's rook move is a little slow. You are doing well — get your king safe and your rooks working.
You castle your king to safety. Solid choice — a safe king lets you play freely.
Big gift! White plays Qxd6 — but his queen can simply be taken. Grab it at once with cxd6.
You snap up the queen with cxd6. Perfect — you spotted the free queen and now you are winning. Lesson: always check if a capture can just be taken back.
White opens with the king pawn. A normal, strong first move.
You play the Sicilian Defense. Great fighting choice that says you want to win, not just draw.
White brings out a knight to a good square. Nothing scary yet.
You develop your knight. Fine and natural.
White builds a small pawn center. A bit slow. You can hit the center soon with d5 or e5.
You develop your knight and poke the e4 pawn. Good, active move.
White pushes the pawn and chases your knight. You must move it now.
Knight to g4 runs to a bad square where it gets chased. Better was Nd5, a calm strong home in the middle. Lesson: when chased, pick a safe square, not a far one.
White plays h3 to kick your knight, but this leaves the e5 pawn loose. Punish it now with Ngxe5 and just win the pawn.
White trades knights.
You take back. You are a clean pawn ahead now.
White pushes to hit your knight and open the center.
You take the pawn. Correct and simple.
White takes with the queen — but the queen comes out too early. Punish it with Nc6, which retreats your attacked knight AND hits the queen, winning time.
You play d6 to guard your knight. It is okay, but Nc6 was stronger: it saved the knight and chased the queen at the same time. Lesson: look for one move that does two jobs.
White gives a check with the bishop. Just block it.
You block the check. Fine and safe.
White trades bishops. This actually helps you a little.
You take back with the queen. Good.
White castles to make the king safe.
You reroute your knight. Solid.
White's queen wanders to the middle and gets loose. Kick it with e6.
You hit the queen with your pawn. Nice, you gain time.
White's queen steps back.
You poke the queen again. Fine, though d5 to open the center was a touch sharper.
White's queen sits far away and looks shaky. Now is a good time to play d5 and grab the center.
You develop your bishop. Okay, but d5 in the center was the stronger plan.
White develops the bishop.
Your bishop steps back to eye the queen. Castling or d5 was a bit more useful.
White's queen returns home.
You castle and tuck your king away safe. Good and healthy.
White develops the last knight.
Knight to the edge pokes the queen, but the rim is a sad square. d5 in the center was better. Lesson: a knight on the side does little.
White's queen slides to safety.
You push e5, which weakens your own squares and lets White's knight target them. d5 was stronger and safer. Lesson: don't push pawns that leave holes behind.
White's knight heads toward your king side. Stay alert — it wants to jump to g5.
You push f5 to grab space. Fine.
White brings a rook to the center.
Rook to e8 looks tidy but takes your eye off your king. Qe6 was better to guard the king side. Lesson: when an attack is near, defend first.
White's knight leaps to g5 and now eyes a deadly Qxh7. You MUST play h6 right now to kick the knight away.
This is the losing move. You missed the threat — h6 was needed to chase the knight and stop the attack. Now White mates. Lesson: before your own move, always ask 'what does my opponent threaten?'
The queen takes with check and the mating attack begins. Your king has to walk.
Forced — the only move.
Another check drives your king forward.
Forced again, your king has nowhere safe.
Checkmate. The whole loss came from move 42: always check the opponent's threat before you push a pawn.
Great start. You open with the king's pawn and grab the center — the best first move.
Your opponent copies you. Now you have a classic open game where both sides fight for the center.
You aim your bishop at the f7 square. Small note: Nf3 first was a touch better to develop and hit the e5 pawn. Lesson: bring out knights before bishops in open games.
They defend e5 with a knight. Nothing scary — just keep developing.
Bringing the queen out this early is risky. Nf3 was better — it develops a piece and the queen can get chased around later. Lesson: develop knights and bishops first, save the queen for later.
They develop their knight and guard key squares. Calm and good for them — keep building your pieces.
Developing the knight is natural, but Ne2 kept things smoother here. Not a big deal. Lesson: try to place knights where pawns can't kick them.
They attack your light bishop with the knight. No panic — just slide the bishop back to safety with Bb3.
Perfect. You save your good bishop on b3 where it still eyes f7.
They make a small luft and prepare to push d5. Solid by them — keep your pieces ready.
Best move. Your knight goes to e2, getting ready to castle and supporting the center.
They play d6 to hold e5, but the stronger d5 was available. Good news for you — you can grab space with d4 next.
Excellent. You strike in the center with d4 and challenge their pawns.
They quietly develop the bishop. Fine for them — get ready to castle and finish developing.
Trading in the center is okay. Castling first (after h3) was a hair cleaner, but this is fine.
They recapture. The center is now settled — time to get your king safe and your rooks active.
The bishop pin looks active, but h3 (making a safe square) was better. The bishop can get pushed around here. Lesson: before pinning, check if they can simply kick your bishop.
They poke your bishop with the h-pawn. Smart move — now retreat to a safe spot like Be3, not h4.
This is the key mistake. On h4 the bishop gets stuck and chased; Be3 kept it safe and useful. Lesson: don't let a piece wander where it can be trapped.
They grab queenside space and miss the sharper Bg4. You can take over the open file with Rd1 right now.
Well done. The rook lands on the open d-file and presses their position.
They develop the bishop to d7. No threat — keep improving your pieces.
Good. You castle and tuck your king away safe behind the pawns.
They trade the knight for your strong bishop. Recapturing toward the center with cxb3 is the cleaner way.
Taking with the a-pawn is okay, but cxb3 was better — it kept your pawns stronger and opened the a-file for your rook. Lesson: usually capture toward the center to keep healthy pawns.
They line up queen and bishop aiming at your kingside. Stay alert — adding defenders and trading their attackers (like Bxf6) keeps you safe.
You start with the king pawn going to the center. A great, normal opening move.
Black plays a fianchetto setup (g6), planning to put the bishop on the long line. This is fine for you — just keep building your center.
Your knight comes out to a good square and guards the center. Solid developing move.
Black puts the bishop on g7, aiming at your center along the long diagonal. Keep an eye on that bishop later — it can be dangerous.
You take the full center with two pawns. Strong move — exactly the plan against this fianchetto setup.
Black plays b6 to also fianchetto the other bishop. This is slow and a little weak — you are ahead in development, so keep developing fast.
You develop the bishop to e3, guarding the d4 pawn. Fine, though bringing the knight to c3 was a touch more natural.
Black puts the bishop on b7, aiming at your e4 pawn. Make sure e4 stays protected as you continue.
Bishop to d3. A small slip — the knight to c3 was better because it develops a new piece and guards e4. Lesson: finish developing your pieces before moving the same bishop around.
Black plays c5 to hit your d4 pawn. Good move by them — now you must decide how to deal with the tension in the center.
You took with dxc5, but this lets Black grab your b2 pawn. The quiet knight to c3 was better, keeping things safe. Lesson: before a capture, check what your opponent can grab back.
Black takes on b2 and now eyes your rook in the corner. You can't easily save the rook, so get the most for it.
Knight to d2 — the best try, getting ready to win the bishop after it takes the rook. Good practical choice.
Black takes your rook in the corner, as expected. Now win that trapped bishop back right away.
Black develops the knight to f6, attacking your e4 pawn. Normal move — make sure e4 is safe and just castle to get your king tucked away.
Knight to g5 was a mistake — it attacks nothing real and wastes time. Simply castling (O-O) was much better and safer. Lesson: don't push a knight forward unless it makes a real threat.
Black castles to safety instead of grabbing the edge. That's a little soft — you got a free moment, so use it to improve your worst piece.
You castled, which is good, but the moment for a kingside pawn push (h4) was even stronger. Still, a safe king is never wrong.
Black takes back the pawn on c5. Now your bishop can recapture and you regain material — take it.
You took on c5 with the bishop. Playable, but pushing e5 to kick the f6 knight was stronger and more active. Keep looking for active pawn pushes in the center.
Black plays d6 to challenge your bishop on c5. Just step the bishop back to a safe, good square.
Bishop back to e3 — a calm, solid retreat that keeps the bishop active. Nice.
Black plays e5, grabbing center space but leaving weak squares behind. This slightly overextends them — your knight can later jump into the holes (like c4 or d5).
You develop the other knight to f3. Fine, though the small move h3 (to stop a knight coming to g4) was a touch cleaner.
Black brings the knight to c6, developing. Quiet move — continue improving your pieces and watch for the bishop swing to h6.

Bishop to g5 pins nothing major and was a little loose; the bishop to h6 (trading Black's strong fianchetto bishop... already gone, so pressuring the king) was better. Keep your bishop on its best diagonal.
Black plays Kg7 to support the kingside and unpin. Normal — just keep building your plan and look at the knight to c4.
Queen to c1 was slow and lets Black play easy moves. The knight to c4, hitting weak squares, was stronger. Lesson: put pieces on active squares, not passive ones.
Black plays h6 to push your bishop away. Step the bishop back to a safe square and keep your structure.
Bishop back to e3. Reasonable, but keeping it on the h4 diagonal stayed more active. Small difference.
Black's rook comes to c8, eyeing the open c-file toward your king side. Watch that file — your c2 pawn and back rank need care.
Knight to b3 was off-target; the knight to c4, jumping into the strong central hole, was clearly better. Lesson: send knights toward weak squares in the enemy camp.
Black plays g5, grabbing space and starting a kingside push. This weakens Black's own king — don't panic and don't grab the pawn without checking the follow-up.
Taking the pawn with Nxg5 was a real mistake — you give up a knight for not enough. Just play h4 to meet the pawn. Lesson: don't sacrifice a piece unless you clearly see what you get back.
Black recaptures on g5 with the pawn, as expected. Now take that pawn back with your bishop to limit the damage.
You take on g5 with the bishop, regaining one pawn. Good — keep your pieces working together.
Black's rook lifts to h8, lining up against your king on the open h-file. Be careful — defend along that file (h4 to block, or trade) soon.
Queen to e3 was a slip that drops your edge; the pawn push h4 to fight for the h-file was much better. Lesson: when an open file points at your king, fight for it fast.
Black retreats the knight to e7, planning to reroute it. You have a moment — grab it by playing f4 to open lines and stay active.
Queen to g3 keeps an eye on the kingside. Okay, but f4, breaking open the center, was the more active choice.
Black's knight heads to g6, aiming at the f4 and h4 squares. Keep your king safe and trade off attackers when you can.
Rook to b1 to use the open b-file. Reasonable, though lining the queen up with Qf3 was a hair better. Fine move.
Black plays Qd7, connecting and preparing to attack. Stay alert on the b7 bishop and the long diagonal toward your king.
Queen to f3 — a solid spot, hitting f6 and helping defense. Good central queen.
Black's knight jumps to h5, attacking your queen and eyeing f4/g3. Move the queen to safety and watch the f4 hole.

The pawn push g4 was a serious mistake — it weakens your king and lets Black's knights swarm in. The knight to a5 (hitting the b7 bishop) was far better. Lesson: don't push pawns in front of your own king when enemy pieces are near.
Black plants a knight on f4, a very strong square next to your king. This is dangerous — try to trade or chase that knight off quickly.
Bishop to f1 was passive and lost ground; the knight to d4 to fight back in the center was better. Lesson: in trouble, look for active defense, not just retreating.
Black grabs your c2 pawn with the rook — a greedy move that you can punish. Trade off the strong f4 knight first with Bxf4 to ease the attack.
Black recaptures on f4 with the other knight, keeping a piece on that strong square. Keep trading attackers and shelter your king.
Queen to e3 was a costly mistake — it lets Black check and win material with Qxg4+. Playing h3 to cover g4 was needed. Lesson: always check what checks your opponent has before moving.
Black checks with Qxg4+ and the attack crashes in. You must block or trade queens right away with Qg3.
Queen to g3 offers a trade and blocks the check — the best practical defense. Good, calm reaction under fire.
Black trades queens with check. This actually helps you a little by removing attackers — recapture and simplify.
You recapture with the pawn, fxg3, fixing your king cover. Trading down is the right idea when you are under pressure.
Black gives a knight check on h3 — you should just take it. Capturing with the bishop is forced and fine.
You take the knight with the bishop, the only good move. Correct — no choice, so play it.
Black takes back on h3 with the rook. The position is messy but playable — bring your pieces to defend the king and the second rank.

Rook to f1 was a blunder that loses the game — it walks into a winning attack. The knight to a1, regrouping, was needed. Lesson: when defending, check that your move doesn't open new lines to your king.
Black takes the e4 pawn and the attack is overwhelming. The game is lost here, but the big takeaway is to keep your king safe and check your opponent's threats before every move.
You start with the king's pawn. Great first move — it grabs the center and opens lines for your pieces.
Your opponent copies you and plays e5. This is a normal open game; just keep developing your pieces.
Black plays d6 to make room for the bishop. This is a quiet, slow move — you can keep developing freely.
Black also puts the queen out on f6, blocking their own knight. This helps you — just develop with Nc3 and play normally.
You move the queen again to b3, keeping the aim at f7. Moving the same piece twice early loses time — Nc3 to develop was cleaner.
Black plays a6, a slow waiting move. No threat to you; just continue with Nf3 and finish your development.
You finally play Nf3. Excellent — this is the best move, getting a piece out and guarding your king's side.
Black plays the slow h6. This does little; you could grab the center with d4 and take a strong hold.
You play the small d3 instead of d4. Pushing d4 was much stronger because it claims the center; d3 is too timid. Lesson: when you can take the center, take it.
Black develops the knight to c6. Normal move — answer by developing too, like Nc3.
Your queen wanders to a4. The queen has moved too many times now; Nc3 to develop a new piece was better. Lesson: get all your pieces out before chasing.
Black blocks with the bishop on d7. Quiet move — you can now reposition your queen or castle soon.
You play Bb5 to pin the knight. It looks active, but keeping things calm with Qb3 was better; this lets Black gain time.
Black develops the second knight to e7. Solid for them — just keep finishing your pieces and think about castling.
You develop the bishop to e3. Not bad, but Nc3 to bring the last knight out was the better builder.
Black's queen goes to g6 eyeing your kingside. Watch your g2 pawn and king safety; castling soon is smart.
You jump the knight to h4 to hit the queen. This pushes the knight to the rim where it does little — castling with O-O was safer and better.
Black retreats the queen to f6. Fine for them; bring your knight back into play with Nf3.
You play g3, weakening the squares around your king. Better was Nf3 to fix the knight first. Lesson: don't loosen pawns near your king without a clear reason.
Black lines the rook up on c8. They are slowly improving; you should trade or castle to get safe.
You grab the a6 pawn with the bishop, but this gives up your good bishop for little. Taking on c6 first was cleaner. Lesson: think before trading your best piece for a pawn.
Black recaptures with the b-pawn, as expected. Now take the pawn back with your queen.
You take the a6 pawn with the queen — the best move, winning the pawn back and staying active.

Your opponent starts with the king pawn, e4. This is the most common first move. It opens lines for the queen and a bishop, and grabs space in the middle.
You play d5, the Scandinavian. It hits the center right away. A small note: c5 was a touch better, but d5 is a fine, fighting choice for your level.
White takes your pawn with exd5. This is normal and expected. Now your pawn is gone, but you can win it back soon.

You take it back with the queen, Qxd5. The queen sits in the open center now. Watch out: White will gain time by attacking your queen, so be ready to move her to safety. Lesson: bringing the queen out early often means it gets chased.
White pushes d4 to build a big center. It also blocks part of the board. You can challenge this center later with pawn breaks like e5 or c5.

You check with Qa5+. It looks active, but it does not really help — White just blocks and your queen wanders. Better was e5, hitting the center while you have the chance. Lesson: a check is only good if it gains something real, not just 'because you can.'
White plays c3 to block your check and support the d4 pawn. This is solid. Your queen on a5 now has fewer good squares, so think about where she goes next.
You develop the knight with Nf6, a good, normal move. It eyes the center and gets you ready to castle.

White plays a3, a slow pawn move that does little. This gives you a free turn — you can grab the center with c5 to hit White's d4 pawn. Lesson: when the opponent plays a slow move, take the chance to improve fast.
You develop with Nc6, putting pressure on the d4 pawn. It is fine, though the pawn push c5 was even stronger to attack the center.
White develops the knight to f3 to guard d4 and get ready to castle. Nothing scary yet. Keep building your own pieces.
You play e5, a strong central break that hits White's d4 pawn. The engine agrees this is the best move. Good job challenging the center.

White grabs your pawn with Nxe5. This is a small slip by White. Just take the knight back with your knight — Nxe5 — and you are doing well. Lesson: when something takes your piece, check if you can simply recapture.
You recapture with Nxe5, the best move. The position stays equal and your knight stands proudly in the center.
You play Qxe5+, taking the pawn back with check. Perfect. Material is even and your queen is active with a tempo.

White plays Be3, which is a real mistake — it blocks nothing useful and drops the lead. The bishop on e3 can be hit. The strong reply is Bc5, pinning that bishop and piling on. Lesson: when the opponent misplaces a piece, attack it fast.
You play Ng4, attacking the e3 bishop. It is okay, but Bc5 was much better — it pinned the bishop and gave you a bigger edge. Still, your knight makes a threat.
You play Nxe3, winning the bishop. Excellent — this is the best move and you grab material.
White recaptures with fxe3, which also opened up White's own king a little. Now your queen can snap the e3 pawn with check ideas. Take it.
You play Bd7, a quiet developing move, but it misses the free pawn. Qxe3 was much better — it wins a pawn and keeps your queen strong. Lesson: look for the capture first before making a calm move.
White castles, O-O, getting the king safe. But White still left that e3 pawn hanging. You can take it with check next.
You play Qxe3+, finally grabbing the loose pawn with check. Good — you are now up material and giving a check too.
White moves the king to h1 to step out of the check. Normal and safe. Keep developing and bring your king to safety soon.
You play Qb6, but this lets White's rook grab your f7 pawn with Rxf7. Better was to castle long, O-O-O, getting your king safe first. Lesson: get your king tucked away before the position opens up.
White plays b4 instead of taking on f7 — a let-off for you. Castle long now with O-O-O to finally make your king safe. Lesson: when given a second chance, take it.
You castle long, O-O-O, the best move. Your king is now safe and your rook joins the game. Well done.
White plays Bf3, aiming at your queenside and the long line. Keep an eye on your b7 and f7 pawns. A queen move like Qh6 keeps you active.

You play Bb5, but this lets White take your b7 pawn with check, Bxb7+. Better was Qh6, keeping your queen active and safe. Lesson: check what the opponent's bishop is aiming at before moving elsewhere.
White plays Bxb7+, winning your b7 pawn with check. You must take the bishop back with your queen, Qxb7, and life goes on. Lesson: always answer a check first.
You play Qxb7, taking the bishop back. Correct — no choice, and you stay in the game.
White gives a check with Qg4+. Just block or step away calmly; Bd7 covers the check nicely. No danger if you stay calm.
You play Kb8, stepping the king aside. It is okay, but Bd7 was a bit cleaner. Your king is tucked in the corner now.

White grabs your f7 pawn with Rxf7, a greedy move that lets you fight back. The engine likes Qd5, centralizing your queen to attack and defend at once. Lesson: when a rook goes pawn-hunting, look for an active queen move.
You play Bd6, eyeing White's king, but Qd5 was stronger to hit more targets at once. Your bishop does point at a nice diagonal though.
White plays Nd2 to bring the last piece out. Solid. The game is now a fight where White has won some pawns, so look for active piece play.
You push h5 to gain a little space, a small slip. Be8 was slightly better to chase the rook. Not a big deal.
White plays Qf5, keeping the queen active. Watch your loose pawns. You can bring a rook to f8 to fight for the open line.
You play Bc6, lining your bishop up on the long diagonal toward White's king. A reasonable, active idea.
White plays Nf3 to reroute the knight. Now you have a nice idea: take the knight with Bxf3, breaking up the pawns near White's king.
You play Rhf8, bringing the rook to the open file. It is fine, though taking on f3 first was a touch sharper. Your rook is now active.
White plays Rxf8, trading rooks. This actually helps you a bit — just recapture. Take back with Rxf8 and keep your pieces working.
You recapture with Rxf8, the best move. Trades are okay here and your rook stays active on the open file.
White plays Qxh5, grabbing a pawn. You have a strong reply: take the knight with Bxf3, smashing the pawns in front of White's king.
You play Bxf3, the best move, breaking up White's pawns near the king. Nicely spotted.
White recaptures gxf3, which leaves White's king more open. Now you can probe with your queen and rook for checks and counterplay.

You play Qxf3+, taking a pawn with check, but trading into a worse endgame. The quiet g6 kept more pressure. Still, you grab a pawn. Lesson: before trading queens, make sure the endgame is good for you.
White takes your queen with Qxf3. Queens are off now. Just recapture and play the rook endgame carefully.
You recapture with Rxf3, the best move. You are now in a rook endgame where careful play matters most.
White pushes the c-pawn, c4, trying to make a passed pawn. Watch this pawn closely — it wants to run forward. Put your rook behind it to stop it.
You play Be5, a good active bishop move. The bishop controls key squares and helps fight White's pawn.
White plays Ra2, a slightly passive rook move. You have time to get active — bring your rook to a strong square like e3.
You play Bd4, centralizing the bishop. It is fine, though a rook to e3 was a touch more active. Your bishop is strong in the middle.
White plays Kg2, walking the king toward the action — normal in endgames. Keep your rook active and watch that c-pawn.
You play Rc3, putting the rook on an active square near White's pawns. Good — active rooks are key in these endings.
White pushes c5, sending the passed pawn forward. This pawn is dangerous, so keep your rook ready to stop or win it. Lesson: a passed pawn must be watched every move.
You play Rc1, but this lets White's king get more active. Keeping your king coming forward with Kb7 was better. Lesson: in endgames, march your king toward the pawns.
White plays h4, starting to push the other pawn. Now you face two ideas to stop, so stay alert and use checks to slow White down.
You play Rg1+, giving a check to bother the king — the best move here. Good idea to use checks to gain time.
White blocks with Kf3. Keep checking or grab the h-pawn when you can. Your rook is doing good work behind enemy lines.
You play Rh1, going after the h4 pawn. The best move — your rook stays busy and wins material.
White plays Kg4 to guard the h-pawn. Now bring your own king up to help; Kb7 is the right plan.
You play Kb7, walking your king toward the action. Exactly right — the king is a strong piece in the endgame.
White plays Rd2, shifting the rook. Stay active. Your bishop and rook can keep making threats while your king marches up.
You play Bf6, lining up to grab the h4 pawn. The best move — your pieces work together well.
White plays Ra2, a passive rook shuffle. You can grab the h4 pawn with check now and pull ahead. Take your chance.
You play Rg1+, a fine check, though grabbing the h-pawn right away with Rxh4+ was just as strong. Your rook keeps the king busy.
White plays Kh3, but this loses time. You can run your king toward the queenside or keep checking to win the h-pawn. Stay active.
You play Rh1+, checking and lining up to win the h-pawn. The best move. Nice and forcing.
White plays Kg4 to guard h4. Now take the pawn with check — Rxh4+ wins it cleanly.
You play Rxh4+, winning the pawn with check. Perfect — material and tempo at once.
White plays Kf5, the only good king move. Keep your rook active and bring your king and pawns into play.
You play Kc6, walking your king toward the center and White's pawns. A good plan in this endgame.
White plays a4, pushing a pawn but leaving the b4 pawn loose. You can grab it with Rxb4. Lesson: when a pawn pushes, check if it left another pawn unguarded.
You play Kd7, but you missed the free pawn on b4. Rxb4 just wins it. Lesson: always look for a loose pawn to grab before moving the king.
White pushes b5, trying to run the pawns. These connected pawns are dangerous now, so stop them with your rook and king together.
You play c6, trying to block, but this helps White's pawns. A rook check first, Rh5+, was better to slow White down. Lesson: be careful pushing pawns near the enemy's runners.
White plays b6, pushing past. The pawns are getting scary. Use your rook from behind and your king up close to hold them.
You play axb6, taking a pawn — a fine practical try to break up White's pawns.
White recaptures cxb6, keeping a dangerous passed pawn on b6. Check with your rook to push White's king back and slow the pawn.
You play Rb4, going after the pawns, but it lets White push a5. A check with Rh5+ first was better to gain time. Your rook does target the pawns though.
White plays a5, supporting the b6 pawn. These pawns are close to queening, so every move counts now. Use checks and your king to fight them.
You play Kc8, bringing the king back to help stop the pawns. Getting the rook checking with Rb5+ was a touch better, but your idea to blockade is right.
White plays Ke6, marching the king up to help its pawns. This is the key danger — White's king supports the runners. Keep your pieces close to stop them.
You play Kb7, putting your king right in front of the pawns to block them. Good defensive idea.
White plays Kd7, a slip that lets you check. A rook check, Rd4+, drives the king back and helps you hold. Lesson: look for a check to push the enemy king away from its pawns.
You play c5, pushing your own pawn, but a rook check, Rd4+, was stronger to slow White. Your pawn does try to make White work.
White plays a6+, pushing the pawn with check. You must move your king now. Be careful — going to the wrong corner can be deadly.
You play Ka8, but this walks into the corner trap. Kb8 was safer and kept you fighting. Lesson: in the corner the king has no air, so avoid it when pawns are pushing.
White plays Kc6, bringing the king up to help mate, but it eases the pressure for a moment. Try to free your bishop and king; Bd8 gives a little defense.
You play Bd8, the best try to guard against the pawns and mate threats. Good defensive resource under pressure.
White plays b7+, pushing with check. This is a sneaky moment — do NOT take the pawn! Step the king to a7 to stay alive. Lesson: when in danger, look at what happens AFTER you capture.

You play Rxb7, but this is the losing move — after axb7+ and Kb8, White plays Ra8 mate. The safe move was Ka7. Lesson: before taking a pawn, ask 'what does my opponent do next?' Taking opened the mate.
White plays axb7+, recapturing with check and setting up mate. Sadly the game is almost over now.
You play Kb8, the only legal move, but mate is coming. Nothing could be done here after the last capture.

White plays Ra8 checkmate. The game is over. Don't be sad — you played a strong middlegame and a clever endgame; just remember to ask 'what comes after I capture?' and to keep your king out of the corner. Well fought!
You open with the King's pawn. It grabs the center and frees your bishop and queen. Lesson: starting in the center is always a good plan.
They copy you, so now it is a normal open game. Just keep bringing out your pieces.
Good. Your knight comes out and attacks their e5 pawn at the same time.
They defend the e5 pawn with their knight. Nothing to fear, keep developing.
This is the Ruy Lopez (Spanish Opening). Your bishop attacks the knight that guards e5. Lesson: this is a strong, classic way to play e4.
They poke your bishop with the pawn. You can keep it by sliding back to a4.
Small slip (Ba4 was better). Trading the bishop so early gives away your strong bishop pair. Lesson: in the Spanish, keep that bishop alive with Ba4.
They take back and open the d-file for their rook. This is fine and normal for them.
You grab the e5 pawn, but it is not really free. After Qd4 their queen hits the knight and the e4 pawn and wins the pawn back. Lesson: castling (O-O) was safer than chasing a pawn.
Their queen jumps to d4 and attacks your knight and the e4 pawn together. Save the knight and you will give the pawn back.
Good. The knight steps to safety and keeps everything defended.
They take the pawn back with check. Just block the check.
Good. You block the check and offer to trade queens.
They trade queens. Take back, the game is now an endgame.
You take back with the king. The king is a bit open but this is okay in an endgame.
Their bishop pins your knight to your king. Kick it away with h3.
Good. You ask the bishop to decide what it wants to do.
They give up the bishop for your knight. Take back, this hands you the two bishops. Lesson: two bishops are a nice long-term edge.
You take back, and your king is active and useful in this endgame.
They castle long and put the rook on the open d-file. Keep developing and watch that file.
Good. A solid pawn move that opens a path for your bishop.
Their bishop gets active aiming at your f2. Keep calmly developing.
Small slip; Nc3 (develop the knight) was a touch better. Still a fine developing move.
They plant the bishop in the center. You can push it back with c3.
You kick the bishop. Fine, though Nc3 was a hair better.
Bishop steps back and you have gained space. Now grab the center.
Good. A strong central pawn that takes lots of space.
They bring the knight back to a better square. Normal play.

They blunder a bit by jumping the knight to d5 (c5 was better). It hits your bishop, so play Nb3 to chase their bishop and keep your edge.
Mistake. Hiding the bishop in the corner is too passive. Lesson: Nb3 was better because it hits their b6 bishop and stays active.
They weaken their king with f5 (c5 was safer). Grab the great central square with Be5.
Mistake. Nb3 was better because it attacks the b6 bishop with tempo. Your bishop also wanted the e5 square.
They tuck the bishop into the corner. Take the strong square now with Be5.
Good. Your knight lands on the powerful e5 square in the center.
Big blunder! With g6 they let your knight fork both rooks. Play Nf7 to win the exchange (rook for knight).
Excellent. The knight forks both rooks on f7 and wins material.
They look for counterplay, but just go take the rook.
Good. You grab the rook in the corner.
They take your knight back, and now you are up the exchange (rook for bishop).
Good. You win a pawn and open lines for your rooks.
They take back, an even trade there. You are still up material.
A bit loose; Be5 (center your bishop) was better. Still fine to use the open file.
Their knight returns to defend and sit in the center.
Slip; Be5 was better to grab the center. Doubling rooks is still okay.
Their knight hops to a strong square and attacks your bishop.
Mistake. Be5 was better, keeping the bishop strong and central. Retreating lets the knight trade itself off well.
They trade their good knight for your bishop, which helps you. Take back toward the center with Kxg3.
Slip; taking with the king (Kxg3) was a bit cleaner to avoid doubled pawns. Still fine.
They push on the queenside. Keep your rooks busy; pushing g4 was the idea.
Mistake. Better was g4 to start rolling your kingside pawns. Your extra material should advance, not drift.
They make a small safety move. Activate your rook with Rd3.
Good. You double your rooks on the open file.
Their king walks toward the center, which is normal in endgames.
Good. A check that pushes their king around.
King steps up. Nothing scary, keep your rooks active.
Slip; Re6+ was better, an active rook check that gains ground. Small pawn moves waste time.
They reroute the bishop. Keep your rooks busy.
Mistake. Re6 was better to keep the rook active and box in the king. This lets them untangle.
They grab the open e-file. Time to push your queenside pawns with b4.
Good plan. You push your queenside pawns forward, the right idea.
They take your pawn. Just recapture.
Good. You take back, the best move.
They slip with b5 (h5 was better). Reposition your rook with R5d3 and keep pressing.
Good. The rook lifts to a better square.
They slip again. Play Rc3+ to check and turn your rook active.
Your biggest mistake. Better was Rc3+ with a check. Pushing g4 lets their rook and pawns get active. Lesson: keep the initiative with checks when you can.
They miss fxg4+ and play Kb6 instead. Just grab the pawn with gxf5.
Good. You take the pawn.
They take back with check. Move your king.
Slip; Ke2 was better, bringing the king in safely. Kg4 lets their pawn give checks.
A check from the pawn. Your king must step over.
Good. The king steps up, the right square.
Bishop check. Move your king again.
Good king move.
Blunder! Now you can win the bishop: play Rxd6+. After cxd6, Rxd6+ wins it all back with profit.
You missed the win here. Rxd6+ (then cxd6, Rxd6+) wins the bishop for nothing. You are still winning, but that was the cleaner shot.
Their bishop checks again from e7. Just move your king; their position is lost anyway.
Good. King steps back, all fine.
Blunder again with Bd6+! This time grab it: Rxd6+, then after cxd6 you play Rxd6+ and win the piece.
Excellent! Now you take the bishop. This wins material and leaves you clearly ahead.
They must take back. Now recapture.
Good. You win the material back and stay well on top.
Their king chases your rook. Move it and start grabbing pawns.
Good. Another pawn falls, and your passed pawns are coming.

Their rook gets active. Keep your pawns rolling.

Their king races over to stop the pawns. Keep them moving.

A rook check. Tuck your king safely to h4.

A small inaccuracy; Rf5 was a hair better, but you are still winning. Keep using your king and rook to walk the passed pawns toward promotion. Lesson: in winning rook endings, let the king and rook escort the pawns home.
You start with the queen's pawn — a calm, solid opening. A fine first move.
Black pushes e5 right next to your pawn — a mistake that just gives a pawn away. Take it: dxe5 wins a free pawn.
