Nice idea — you get your bishop to f5 outside the pawn wall, just in time. This is exactly the right way to play this kind of locked position.
White builds a strong pawn center with d4. Keep developing and look for breaks like f6 or c5 later to hit it.
You bring the knight to c6 to add pressure on d4. Playing e6 first was a touch cleaner, but this is okay.
White plays c3 to defend the d4 pawn. Nothing scary — just keep getting your pieces out.
You play e6 to support your center and open a path for your dark bishop. Solid and safe.
White develops the knight to f3. Calm move; continue your own plan.
Small mistake: g6 is slow and does not fight the center. Better was f6, hitting the e5 pawn right away — when the center is locked, you must challenge it, not play around the edge.
White offers to trade your good bishop with Bd3. You can take it, since that bishop has done its job.
Good — you trade on d3. Clean and simple, no problems.
White takes back with the queen. Keep finishing your development.
You put the bishop on g7, pointing across the long line. Good spot for it.
White castles to safety. Time for you to get your king safe too and think about the f6 break.
You bring the knight to h6, heading for f5. A bit slow — f6 to strike the center was stronger, but this is minor.
White lines the rook up on the e-file. No threat yet; just be aware that file may open later.
You castle and get your king safe. A small note: a5 was a bit more active, but safety is never wrong.
White plays Bg5, eyeing your queen's side and the e-file. Be careful — don't open the position while White is more ready.

Big mistake: f6 opens the game right when White is lined up on the e-file. After White takes, the trades win material for White — the safe move Qe8 kept everything solid. Lesson: don't break open lines when the enemy rooks and bishop point at your king.
White takes on f6 as expected. You must take back, but the damage is already done.
You recapture on f6 with the rook. This is forced and the best you have now.
White grabs your rook with the bishop. It looks scary, but you win the bishop right back, so it is not a clean loss.
Good — you take the bishop with your queen. You got some material back; stay calm and play on.
White makes luft with h3 to give the king air. Quiet move; improve your worst piece.
Mistake: pushing e5 loses a pawn after White takes. Nf5 was better, putting your knight on a strong square — when behind, keep your pawns safe instead of pushing.
White takes your pawn on e5. You need a way to win it back, but be careful how.
Mistake: Nxe5 drops the knight, because White can answer Rxe5 and win it. Qe6 first was the safe path — always check if the square you take on is defended.
White takes your knight back. You are now down material, so look for active checks and trades to fight on.
You play Re8 to pin White's knight to the rook. Good — this is your best try to win the piece back.
Blunder by White: f4 hangs the pawn while the knight is pinned. Take it now with Qxf4 — the knight cannot move, so the pawn is free.
You grab the f4 pawn with the queen. Well spotted — that wins back some material.
White moves the knight to f3, a little loose. Trade rooks first with Rxe1+ to simplify.
You check and trade rooks with Rxe1+. Smart — when you are fighting, fewer pieces can help.
White takes back with the knight. Keep your remaining pieces active and your pawns safe.
Mistake: pushing d4 sends the pawn too far forward where it can be attacked. Better was c6 to keep it protected — loose pawns become easy targets in the endgame.
White plays Nf3 to attack your d4 pawn. Defend it actively with a check like Qc1+ before White can win it.
You start with the king pawn. A great, strong opening that grabs the center right away.
Your opponent plays the Sicilian Defense (the c5 push). It is normal here. Just keep building your pieces toward the center.
You bring out your knight to a good square. Nice and natural development.
They develop their knight too. No threat yet. Keep getting your pieces out and think about safety.
You point your bishop at their side. Fine, but Bb5 (pinning their knight) is the cleaner spot. Small thing, not a real mistake.
They open a small home for their bishop. Calm move. Carry on developing.
You push in the center to open lines. A reasonable idea; Nc3 was a touch tidier. Lesson: develop a piece before opening the middle.
They match you in the center. Things are about to trade off. Keep your pieces connected.
Good capture. You take cleanly and keep the position simple.
They take back. The center is now open and even. Time to finish developing.
You play Bb5 to press their knight, the idea from move 5. Nice plan.
They push a6 to kick your bishop — but this is a small slip by them. Best for you is Bxc6+: take the knight with check and mess up their pawns.

This is the big one. Retreating to a4 lets b5 trap your bishop and you lose a lot. Better was Bxc6+ taking the knight with check. Lesson: when a pawn attacks your bishop, check if you can grab a piece first.
They play b5 and your bishop is in real trouble. Try to save the game with c4 to fight back in the center.
Qe2+ gives a check, but it does not help much. c4 was stronger to hit back at their pawns. Lesson: a check is only good if it leads somewhere.
They block the check with the bishop. Now is your chance: play c4 to open the center and win material back.
Good — you grab the b5 pawn and get some of your lost material back. Smart recovery.
They take back with the pawn. As planned, you should recapture with Qxb5. Stay calm and keep grabbing what you can.
You take with the queen and win the pawn. Well done climbing back into the game.
They move their queen to d7 to guard. No threat to you. You can keep grabbing the loose c5 pawn.
They take your knight on d4. The best answer is Qxd7+ — trade queens first with check, then take the knight back.
You take the knight back. Good, you keep the material even.
They recapture with the pawn. The position is steady. Now bring your last pieces into play.
Strong move. Your queen sits on d3 on a great central square. Engine's top pick.
They place their bishop actively. No threat. Just keep developing and connect your rooks.
Bf4 develops with a little annoyance. Fine, though Nd2 was smoother to bring the knight in. Small thing.
They play Nf6 — a slip that costs them. The clean reply is Nd2, bringing your knight toward the action and keeping your strong setup.
You play Nd2 as planned. Perfect — your knight heads to a better square.
They castle to safety. No danger to you. Keep improving your worst piece.
Nf3 lets some of your edge slip. Nb3 was better, hitting their d4 pawn and eyeing strong squares. Lesson: aim your knight where it attacks something.
They tuck their queen to a7. Quiet move with no threat. Calmly continue your plan and keep your pieces working together.
You start with d4. Good first move, you take space in the middle.
Black plays e6. This is calm. You can grab the center with e4 next.
You play e4! Now you have two big pawns in the center. This is the strong plan. Lesson: two center pawns give you space and freedom.
Black plays a6, a slow side move. It does little. You just keep building your pieces.
You develop your bishop to d3, aiming at Black's king side. Nice and natural.
Black plays d6, a small pawn move. Keep developing; your center is still bigger.
You play Nf3. Perfect — your knight comes out and guards the center. Lesson: bring knights and bishops out early.
Black plays h6, another slow pawn move. Black is wasting time, so keep getting ready.
You castle (O-O). Your king is safe and your rook is ready. Always good.
Black plays b6 to fianchetto a bishop. Calm. Keep improving your pieces.
You play Nc3. Fine development, though Be3 was a touch better. No real harm.
Black plays Bb7, pointing the bishop at your center. Watch your e4 pawn; it is fine for now.
You play Be3, finishing development. Good — all your pieces are out and your king is safe.
Black plays Nd7. Black is cramped and slow. A good plan for you is to push d5 to gain space.
You play Qe2. Okay, but pushing d5 right away was stronger to grab more space. Lesson: when you have more room, use a pawn push to squeeze your opponent.
Black plays g6, making a home for the bishop. Keep loading your rooks onto good lines.
You play Rad1. Great — the rook sits behind your d-pawn, ready for the d5 break.
Black plays Be7 instead of Ne7, a slip that loses time. Now d5 or Nd2 grabs the edge.
You push d5! You gain space and lock in your advantage. Good use of the rook you set up on move 17.
Black plays e5, closing the center. Now both sides will play on the wings; you have the better space.
You play Nd2 to reroute the knight, but a4 (gaining queenside space) was stronger. Small misstep. Lesson: when the center is closed, grab space on the side with pawns.
Black plays Bc8, sending the bishop back home. This is very passive and helps you. Keep improving.
You play f4, hitting Black's e5 pawn. A strong break that opens lines for your rook and pieces.
Black plays Nb8, putting the knight in the corner — a bad move that wastes time. Punish it: take with fxe5 to open the center while you are better developed.
You play fxe5! Exactly right — you open the f-file and the center.
Black recaptures dxe5. Normal. Now your pieces are more active.
You play Nc4, eyeing weak squares, though lining up the queen with Qf2 was a touch sharper. Still fine.
Black plays f6 to hold the e5 pawn, but it weakens his king. The strong push was d6 to break things open; keep that idea in mind.
You play Qf3. A small inaccuracy — the pawn push d6 was much stronger, cracking Black open. Lesson: a passed pawn that can push deep is often worth more than slow moves.
Black plays h5, a loosening pawn move that ignores danger. Punish it: Nxe5! wins the e5 pawn and opens lines.
You play Nxe5! You win a pawn and your pieces come alive. Well spotted.
Black plays Bg4 to chase your knight, but it just trades into your favor. Take it: Nxg4.
You play Nxg4, winning the bishop trade cleanly. Good and simple.
Black recaptures hxg4. Now grab the loose pawn.
You play Qxg4, winning the g4 pawn. You are now clearly ahead in material. Nice clean play.
Black plays g5, a weak pawn push that drops material. Punish it: push e5 to open the way to Black's king.
You play e5! Strong — you open lines straight toward Black's exposed king. Good plan.
Black plays Rh4, a strange rook move that hangs the king. Punish it: Bg6+ gives check and wins.
You play Bg6+! A great check that traps Black's king. Very strong.
Black plays Kf8, forced. Now keep pressing; grabbing the g5 pawn with Qxg5 was the cleanest.
You play Qe6. This lets the win slip — Qxg5 was far stronger, keeping the attack rolling. Lesson: in attacks, grab loose pawns and keep your pieces working together.
Black plays Nh6, another weak move. Now Bxg5 is strong, winning a pawn and keeping the heat on Black's king.
You play d6! A powerful pawn push deep into Black's side. This pawn becomes a monster.
Black plays cxd6 — a huge blunder. Punish it: Bxg5! wins material and your attack crashes through.
You play exd6, which is okay but Bxg5 was crushing. You are still winning big; keep it simple.
Black plays Ra7, a sad defensive move. You are far ahead. Bxg5 keeps cleaning up; trading down also wins.
You play dxe7+, a check that trades queens. It works, but Bxg5 kept more. Still, simplifying when ahead is fine. Lesson: when you are way ahead, trading pieces makes winning easier.
Black plays Qxe7, forced recapture. Now trade queens with Qxe7+ to make the win easy.
You play Qc8+ instead of trading queens. A small slip — Qxe7+ was cleaner. You are still clearly winning.
Black plays Kg7, the only square. Keep your pieces active and bring in your knight.
You play Bf2, a quiet move. The knight jump Nd5 was sharper, but you are still well ahead.
Black plays Rf4, an active rook try. Now Nd5 is strong, hitting the rook and gaining ground.
You play Nd5! Good — your knight jumps to a great central square with threats.
Black plays Qb7, offering a queen trade. Take it: Qxb7+ trades into an easy winning endgame.
You play Nxf4 instead, which lets Black grab your queen — a costly slip. Trading queens with Qxb7+ was much safer. Lesson: when way ahead, trade queens to kill all counterplay.
Black plays Qxc8, taking your queen as planned. You are still ahead on pieces; stay calm and trade.
You play Nh5+, a check, but quietly improving with Rd8 was better. Small inaccuracy.
Black plays Kxg6, grabbing your bishop. Now win the f6 pawn with Nxf6 and keep your edge.
You play Ng3, retreating, when Nxf6 grabbed a pawn and stayed active. Minor slip; you are still better.
Black plays Qxc2, grabbing a pawn. Stay steady — centralize your rook with Rd6 to keep control.
You play Bxb6, taking a pawn, though Rd6 (activating the rook) was a bit better. Still fine.
Black plays Rb7 to defend. Now Bd4 puts your bishop on a strong diagonal toward Black's king.
You play Bd4! Great square — the bishop aims right at Black's king side. Good plan.
Black plays Nc6, hitting your bishop. You can keep the bishop strong; Bc3 holds the diagonal.
You play Rxf6+, grabbing a pawn with check, but keeping rooks back with Rff1 was stronger. Small slip; still playable.
Black plays Kh7, the only move. Keep your pieces coordinated and press on.
You play Rxh6+, a rook sacrifice for the knight, but it gives up too much — Rff1 kept your big edge. Be careful trading your active pieces away.
Black plays Kxh6, taking the rook as forced. Now you have a knight check; use it.
You play Nf5+, a check that wins Black's queen for your knight. A clever trick to grab the queen.
Black plays Qxf5, forced to give the queen. Now push your h-pawn (h4) to attack Black's pawns.
You play Bf2, a quiet move, when h4 was more active hitting Black's pawns. Small inaccuracy.
Black plays Qc2, eyeing your pawns. Stay calm — a rook check like Rd6+ keeps things in hand.
You play Rd6+, a check to push Black's king. This drives the king and keeps you active.
Black plays Kh7, the only square. Keep your king safe; h4 was a good, simple plan.

You play Rf6??, a big blunder — it hangs your bishop and lets Black's queen check in. Watch for back-rank and check tricks. Lesson: before moving, always ask 'does this leave a piece loose or my king open?'
Black plays Qd1+, a strong check that wins your bishop. You must block.
You play Be1, forced to block the check with the bishop. No choice here.
Black plays Qxe1+, taking your bishop with check. You have to deal with the check now.
You play Rf1, blocking the check. This is the only good move and saves you from worse. Good.
Black plays Qe3+, another check. Tuck your king away safely.
You play Kh1, stepping the king to safety. Correct and forced.
Black plays Rxb2, grabbing a pawn. The game is very hard for you now; keep your king safe and look for checks to trade pieces. Lesson: stay calm in tough spots and make your opponent prove the win.
You start with the king pawn to the center. A strong, normal first move.
Black plays the Sicilian, pushing a pawn to fight your center. Just keep developing your pieces calmly.
You bring out your knight to a good square. Nice and natural.
Black develops a knight too. Both sides are building up, so keep going.
You put your bishop out, but Bb5 was a bit better here because it pins and pressures the knight. Still fine, no harm done.
Black makes room for his own bishop. Nothing scary, just continue.
You push to the center to open things up. Nc3 was a touch smoother, but this is okay.
Black takes your pawn, which is expected. Take it back with your knight next.
You recapture with the knight, sitting it on a strong central square. Good.
Black puts a bishop on an active diagonal. You can trade off his knight to mess up his pawns.
You take the knight, the engine's top choice. This doubles black's pawns and weakens him.
Black takes back, now with two weak pawns side by side. You did well, keep pressing them.
You castle and tuck your king safely away. Always a good idea.
Black's queen move is a small mistake; d5 was better for him. You could have hit his queen with Qg4. Lesson: when the enemy queen comes out early, look for a move that chases it.
You develop the last knight. A calm, solid choice that keeps everything together.
Big mistake by black! His bishop move loses a lot. You can win material with Na4, attacking his bishop on c5. Lesson: when your opponent blunders, slow down and hunt for the move that wins a piece.
You trade bishops instead, which lets black off the hook. Na4 was much stronger because it forked and won his bishop. Lesson: a capture is not always best — check if a quieter move wins more.
Black takes back with his queen, and the position is level again. Keep playing solid moves.
Your bishop move was passive; e5 was much better, grabbing space and freeing your pieces. Lesson: in the middlegame, look for pawn pushes that open lines for you.
Black trades bishops, which is fine for him. Take back and keep your structure.
You recapture with the pawn. This is the right way, keeping your pawns connected.
Black's knight move is a little slow; Nh6 was better for him. Keep building your pieces toward his king.
Your queen move drifts a bit; Qd4 was better, sitting strong in the center. Lesson: put your queen where it controls the most squares.
Black castles to safety. Now both kings are tucked in, so play on the open lines.
You bring your rook to the open file. Good plan, rooks love open lines.
Black shuffles his queen back. You can jump your knight to a4 to poke at him.
You play the knight to a4, eyeing weak squares. Nice and active.
Black's queen slides over to defend. Keep improving your pieces and add pressure.
You play b3 to make a safe home for your knight and guard your pawns. Solid.
Black doubles rooks on the open file; d5 was a bit better for him. Stay alert to his pressure down that file.
Your knight retreat lets black get active; Qg3 was better, keeping your queen aggressive. Lesson: try not to step backward when you can keep the pressure on.
Black's queen swings to c5. Watch that diagonal and keep your pieces coordinated.
Your rock move was a bit awkward; Na4 was better, hitting the queen. Lesson: with your knight on the edge, use it to attack, not just sit.
Black's knight comes to g6, heading for active squares. Be careful, it may jump in.

Serious slip! Stacking rooks here drops material — Qe2 was needed. Now black's knight can leap to e5 and win your rook for a knight. Lesson: before a quiet-looking move, check what your opponent's knight can jump to.
Black's knight lands on e5 and now forks your rook. You must save the rook or accept losing the exchange.
Another costly move; Qe2 was much safer. Now black has Nxf3+, a check that wins a pawn and breaks up your king. Lesson: when your king's pawns are loose, watch for knight checks.
Black takes with check, grabbing a pawn and exposing your king. Take the knight back right away.
You recapture with the pawn. Correct, but sadly your king is now drafty.

Black grabs another pawn with his queen — but this was greedy, Qe7 was better. You can play R3d2 to trap and trade off his queen. Lesson: a deep-diving queen can get trapped, so look for moves that box it in.
Big blunder — your knight move hangs the piece. R3d2 was the move, going after his queen. Now black just takes your knight for free. Lesson: never leave a piece where the enemy queen can grab it.
Black takes your knight, winning a clean piece. The game is hard now, but keep fighting.
Taking the pawn loses more; Kh1 was safer to tuck your king. Now black has checks coming. Lesson: when behind, keep your king safe before grabbing pawns.
Black takes your rook on d7. Take his rook back to trade down.
You recapture the rook. A fair trade, though you are still down material.

Black checks your king and will scoop up your weak pawns. The position is lost, but you played a brave game — the big lessons are to slow down on quiet moves and watch for knight jumps and checks near your king.
White starts by taking the middle with a pawn. Calm move — you can grab the center too.
You put your pawn in the middle to meet White. This is a solid Queen's Pawn opening. Lesson: fighting for the center early is always a good plan.
White makes a small quiet move and shuts in one bishop. Nothing scary — just keep developing.
Your knight comes out, but it blocks your own c-pawn. A bit better was Nf6, sending the knight toward the center and your king. Lesson: try not to block your own pawns.
White brings out a knight, normal and good. Now you bring your pieces out too.
Your knight jumps to a strong square and watches the center. Nice, clean development.
White develops another knight; a slightly slow choice. You are doing fine — keep going.
You open a path for your dark bishop. Solid and natural.
White plays a slow side-pawn move. Slow for them means free time for you.
Your bishop goes to an active square aiming at White's king side. Best spot for it.
White's bishop goes to a passive square. That gives you an easy extra move.
You castle and tuck your king away safe. Always a good idea.
White's bishop goes to a quiet square. Nothing to worry about.
Your rook lines up on the e-file for a future push. Fine; a6 (stopping White's knight jump) was also nice.
White castles and gets safe too. Game is even.
You push in the center to open lines for your pieces. Good, active break. Lesson: a strong central pawn push frees your bishops and rooks.
White trades pawns in the middle. Just take back.
You take back with the knight, landing it on an active center square. Good recapture.
White trades knights, which actually helps you (about two-thirds of a pawn given away). Take back with Bxe5 — your bishop becomes a monster in the center.
You recapture and your bishop now rules the middle of the board. Strong and exactly right.
White's bishop eyes your queenside and your d-pawn. Keep your center pawn protected.
You support your center and grab a little space. Fine; c6 was a touch safer.
White makes a little air hole for the king. A slow move — you can keep building.
Your bishop comes out and guards your d-pawn — natural. The engine liked the quiet h6 just a hair more, but this is fine.
White retreats the bishop all the way home — very passive, almost a free move for you. Punish it by improving: Bc7 keeps your bishop aimed at White's king.

You push your pawn forward, but it just gets traded and opens lines for White (about three-quarters of a pawn lost). Better was Qd6, lining your queen up toward White's king. Lesson: don't push a pawn that the enemy can simply swap off.
White trades the pawns. Take back with the c-pawn.
You recapture cleanly. Good.
White's knight leaps to a central square and offers a trade.

You trade knights, but this lets White's bishop get strong on e4 aiming at your king (about half a pawn lost). Better was Bf5, developing with a pin and keeping pieces on. Lesson: trading can help your opponent's other pieces.
White takes back, and now that bishop stares at your h7 square. Watch your king side.
Your queen comes out and eyes the long diagonal toward White's king. Fine; Bc7 was a touch better.
White's queen move is a big blunder! Play Bc4 — your bishop attacks the queen and White can't comfortably save it.
Bc4! Your bishop attacks White's queen and grabs the upper hand. Exactly the right punch. Lesson: when a piece is attacked and can't escape well, you win material.
White grabs your h-pawn with a check instead of saving the queen — a trick to confuse you. Stay calm: just step the king to h8.
King to h8 keeps you safe and your bishop still hunts the queen. Cool head, well done.
White's queen runs to e4 — a big blunder! Hit it with Bh2+: after the king moves, Rxe4 wins the whole queen.
You took the rook instead and missed the bigger prize (over three pawns lost). Bh2+ first would have won White's queen. Lesson: always check for a check that wins even more.
White takes your bishop back. You're still doing well — bring more pieces in. Bf6 was the strong square.
This check just gets blocked and helps White trade (over three pawns lost). Better was Bf6, centralizing with threats. Lesson: a check that does nothing can waste a good position.
White blocks the check and offers to swap queens.
You pull the queen back and keep queens on the board. Best choice.
White's bishop sits in the center. Keep an eye on it.
Your bishop takes a nice diagonal, but Bf4 (offering to trade off White's bishop) was sharper. Small slip.
White's queen move is a huge blunder! Play Qe5 — it hits the e4 bishop twice and wins it.
You missed it — Qh2 lets White start checking your king (over five pawns lost). Qe5 would have won the free bishop. Lesson: before attacking, scan for a piece you can simply win.
White checks your king. Step away with Kg8.
King to g8, the safe square. Forced and correct.
White checks again, chasing your king.
You walk the king to f8 and out of the checks. Good, basically the only move.
White develops the bishop. Quiet move.
This pawn move wastes time (over one pawn lost) — you had Qh1+! That check leads to grabbing White's rook on a1. Lesson: look for your own checks before slow pawn moves.
White's pawn push is a big blunder! Now Qh1+ followed by taking on a1 wins a whole rook.
Qh1+! Your queen checks and heads straight for the loose rook. Great, you found it.
White's king steps away but can't defend the rook.
Qxa1 wins the rook — a big chunk of material! Now you are clearly ahead.
White's bishop move drops material — a blunder! Play Rxe4+: you win the bishop with check.
Rxe4+! You take the bishop with check and you are completely winning. Lesson: when you're ahead, keep grabbing free pieces with checks. Well played at the finish.
Your opponent starts with the pawn on d4. This is a calm, normal start. Just build your pieces in the center.
You answer d5 and meet them in the center. Good, solid, and equal.
They play Bf4 to put the bishop on a free, open spot. Nothing to fear here.
Nc6 develops, but Nf6 was a touch better because it helps guard your d5 pawn. Small thing, not a real error.
They bring out the knight to c3. They are pressing on your d5 pawn now, so keep it defended.

Nf6 develops, but watch out: their knight can jump to b5 and poke at your weak c7 square. Try to deal with that idea early. Lesson: when a square near your king is loose, the enemy knight loves to land there.
As feared, the knight hops to b5 and eyes c7. You can hit back in the center with e5 right away.
e5! Nice. You strike the center and chase the f4 bishop at the same time. Best move.
They take dxe5. The pawn trade is fine for you. Now try a6 to kick the b5 knight away.
Nh5 attacks the f4 bishop, but a6 first was better to chase the dangerous b5 knight off c7. Lesson: shoo away the piece that is aiming at your weak square first.
They play e3 to open their bishop and hold things together. Calm move; you can win the bishop pair with Nxf4.
Nxf4 takes the bishop. A clean, fair trade. Good.
They take back exf4. Even trade, nothing scary.
Bc5 looks active, but it drops your d5 pawn — after Qxd5 you are just a pawn down. Better was to keep d5 safe. Lesson: before an attacking move, check what you leave undefended behind you.
They grab the free d5 pawn with Qxd5. You are down a pawn now, so play tight and don't give more away.
Qe7 is loose — it lets their knight take on c7 with check and grab even more. Bb6 was safer. Lesson: with the enemy knight near your king, guard c7 before anything else.
Their knight takes c7 with check and also hits your loose pieces. You must move the king to f8 and stay calm.
Qxc7 saves the knight but now your bishop on c5 falls. Moving the king to f8 lost less. You are dropping more material here.
They take your bishop with Qxc5. You are down a good amount of material now; play for tricks and trades to survive.
Be6 develops and is fine. Just keep getting pieces out and your king safe.
They play Nf3 to develop. Quiet move; carry on getting your king tucked away with castling.
O-O-O! Good — your king finally finds a home and your rook joins the game.
They put the bishop on c4 to trade off your good bishop. You can take it, or sidestep — either is okay.
Bxc4 trades bishops. Fine and simple, fewer pieces helps the side that is behind a little.
They take back Qxc4. Calm spot now; keep your pieces working together.
Qa5+ gives a check but it wastes time and drifts offside. Nd4 was stronger, jumping to a strong central square. Lesson: a check that leads nowhere just helps the other side.
They block with c3, gaining time on your queen. Bring the queen back to a useful spot.
Rd5 is active but a little loose. The position is roughly holding; keep your pieces guarded.
They castle to safety with O-O. Good moment for you to trade queens and ease the pressure.
Rc5 misplaces the rook and drops your f7 pawn. Rhd8 keeping rooks active was better. Lesson: don't leave back pawns hanging while your rook wanders.
They snap up the free f7 pawn with Qxf7. You are slipping further behind; bring the rook back and stay solid.
Rd8 retreats, but it lets their plan roll on. The rook had better squares. You are under real pressure now.
They push e6 and overpush — this actually hands you a chance with Rf5 to hit their loose pawns. Don't miss it!
Qc7 offers a queen trade, which is smart when you are behind — fewer pieces means fewer dangers.
They trade queens with Qxc7+. Good for you; the attack on your king is gone now.
Kxc7 takes back. Now it is just a rook endgame; activity and your passed b-pawn are your hope.
They double... I mean place a rook on e1. They want the open file. Get your king active and your rook busy.
Re8 trades on the open file, but marching the king up with Kd6 was more useful. In endings the king must help. Lesson: in rook endings, walk your king toward the action.

They take back. Even trade — now use your queen actively, like Qe5.
The rook to g1 was okay, but pushing c4 was a bit stronger to open lines. No real harm.
They make a quiet pawn move and weaken their king. You can jump in with Rg6 to attack. Rg6!
Your queen comes to a strong central square. Good, it eyes their king and pawns.
They defend with the rook. Press on — Rg7 keeps them tied down.
Playing f4 was too slow and lets them off the hook; Rg7 kept them pinned. Lesson: keep the squeeze on, don't release the pressure.
They push c5 and badly weaken their king — f5 next breaks things wide open. Play f5!
Bh7 wanders the bishop away; the pawn break f5 was crushing. Lesson: when you can blast open the king, do it.

They recapture. Now go for the rook check — Rg7+.

Their king steps the wrong way (Ke8). Now snatch the loose knight with Rxa7! Rxa7.
They blunder again with Rf7 — your bishop trick Bg6 wins the pinned rook. Play Bg6!

Their king steps up. Now push f5 to open lines and use your bishop.
Bg6 is okay, but pushing f5 was stronger to break through. Minor slip.
They block with the rook. Push f5 now to make progress.

Their king blocks. Keep the rook active — Rg8 lines up nicely.

They grab your f-pawn. Fine — give the check Rg7+ and keep driving the king.
Bringing the king up was slow; Rg7+ first kept them pinned. Lesson: check to push the king before walking your own king up.
They push the a-pawn to run it. Stop it — Ra8 gets behind the runner.
The bishop check helps a bit, but going behind the pawn with Ra8 was stronger. Small slip.
Their king hides on c7. Check with Rg7+ to chase it and stay in control.
Bb5 is okay, but Rg7+ kept the attack flowing. Minor inaccuracy.

Their king wanders to b7. Now check with Rg7+ and herd it.
You give the rook check. Right on target.

Their king steps to c7. Now win the b-pawn with Bxb5.

They grab your f-pawn. Let it go — keep your rook active with Ra6.
Be8 wandered the bishop off; Ra6 kept your rook strong. Lesson: keep your rook active in the endgame, don't drift. Still winning.
They take your h-pawn. No worry — get the rook to a6 and push your own plan.
Bg6 is okay, but the king march with Kd6 was a touch better. Minor slip — you have a winning game.
They check your king. Just step away with Kb2 and keep pushing your win.

You bring the bishop back to d1, keeping it flexible and eyeing key squares. Good, no loss.

Black takes your knight. Just recapture with exf5 and your pawns gain a strong post.

Black lifts a rook to g5. A little loose. You can grab the a5 pawn with Qxa5 and stay clearly better.

You take the a5 pawn at last. Good to win it, though the queen capture Qxa5 was a bit cleaner.
Black slides the bishop to b6 with some pressure. Calmly play Ra6 to hit the bishop and keep your rook active.
You hit the black bishop with your rook on a6. Strong, best move, gaining time.

You center your queen on a1, eyeing the long diagonal toward black's king. Fine move with no loss.

You put the bishop on f3, a great diagonal pointing at black's king side. Good developing of the attack.
Black's queen step is a small slip. You can play Qd1 to pile up and keep the pressure on.
This rook move lets black grab your f5 pawn. Qd1 was better, holding everything together. Be careful giving up pawns near a sharp position.
Black takes the f5 pawn with the queen. The position is sharp now — keep your pieces coordinated and watch both kings.
This rook grab is a serious blunder that hangs material and lets black attack. Be4 was the safe, strong move. Lesson: in sharp spots, check your king's safety before grabbing.
Black grabs the h3 pawn but this is also a big blunder! You have a winning shot: Rh7+! After Kxh7 Be4+ f5, you crash through to the black king.
You defend with the queen to f1. Okay, but Rh7+ was a crushing attack — don't forget forcing checks. Still, you are fine.
Black pulls the queen back to defend. The storm calmed a bit. Now develop your bishop to its strong diagonal.
You plant the bishop on d5, a powerful diagonal aiming near black's king. Strong and best.
Black's queen move to f5 is a mistake. Hit it with Be4! After h4 Bxf5 Rxf5, you win the queen for less and stand much better.
You play Be4, attacking the black queen and taking control. Excellent, the best move.
Black's queen move walks into mate! Black needed to take your bishop. Now you deliver checkmate.
Rh7 checkmate! Your rook lands next to the black king with no escape. Well played at the end — a clean finish.
You start with the king pawn going to the middle. A great first move that grabs the center and frees your pieces.
Black plays a quiet pawn to d6. This is a slow setup, so you can keep taking the center with d4.
You push the second center pawn to d4. Now you own the whole middle of the board — exactly the right plan.
Black plays c6 to make a little box for the king. It is slow, so just keep building your pieces.
You bring out your knight to c3, aiming at the center. Calm and correct development.
Black puts the queen on c7 early. The queen does little here, so keep developing and grab space.
You move the bishop to f4, but the engine liked the pawn push f4 better. Bf4 lets Black hit your bishop with a pawn later. Lesson: in this setup, the pawn to f4 builds a strong wall and gains space.
Black develops the knight to d7. Nothing scary — finish getting your pieces out.
You place the bishop on d3, eyeing Black's king side. A fine, safe developing move.
Black pushes e5 to fight for the center and hits your d4 pawn. You must decide how to deal with the tension.
You take with dxe5, but keeping the bishop active with Be3 was a touch better. Trading eases the center too soon. Lesson: don't release tension unless it helps you; sometimes just hold and develop.
Black takes back with the pawn, dxe5. The center is now open and even. Keep finishing development.
You slide the bishop to g3, tucking it safely. A reasonable retreat that keeps the bishop alive.
Black develops the knight to f6, attacking your e4 pawn. Notice e4 now needs an eye kept on it.
You develop the knight to f3 to get ready to castle. Solid, though h3 to stop a knight jump was also nice.
Black puts the bishop on c5, an active spot. Keep an eye on your f2 pawn and just castle.
You castle and tuck your king safe. Good — king safety first.
Black castles too. Both kings are home; now it's about plans and piece play.
You move the bishop to c4, pointing at Black's f7. An active idea, aiming at the weak f7 square.

You play Rc1, but stopping Black's pawns with a4 was much better. Now Black gets to push b5 with space. Lesson: when the other side wants to storm pawns at you, block them early instead of slow rook moves.
Black pushes b5, gaining space on the side and chasing your bishop. Step the bishop back to safety.

Black takes your bishop with the king, Kxf7. The smoke clears; the game is close to level.

Black takes the knight with gxh6, opening his own king wide. Now pile in with checks: Qg4+ is the move.

Black plays Kf7, stepping out, and now stands better. Steady yourself and look for safe checks to hold the draw.
You play Qc7+, a check, but the quiet g3 was steadier. The check chases but gains little. Lesson: aimless checks waste time — make sure each check leads somewhere.
Black plays Ke8, walking the king up the board. Keep checking safely or grab a pawn to stay alive.
You play Qxc6+, taking a pawn with check. Good — you win material and keep the king busy.
Black blocks with Kf7. Keep the checks coming and look to win more pawns.

Black blocks with Be7. Keep an eye on your back rank and your b2 pawn now.

Black plays Qc1+, checking and heading for your weak pawns. You must step the king out of check.
You play Kg2, the right square out of check. Good — your king is safe for now.
Black plays Qxb2, grabbing your pawn. The game is about even here — stay calm, keep your king safe, and look for checks or trades to hold.
Your opponent opens with the king's pawn. This is the most common first move. Be ready for an open, active game.
You answer in the center with your own pawn. This is a solid, classic reply.
They develop a knight and attack your center pawn. Now you should defend it.

You develop your knight and attack their e4 pawn. Smart, you add pressure to the center.

You castle to safety, but you missed the free pawn. Nxe4 was clearly better because it wins a pawn for nothing.

You take the d4 pawn. This is fine, though stepping the bishop back to b6 was a touch better.

They push e5, but this loses a pawn. Take it for free with dxe5 — the pawn is not properly protected.

White moves the king pawn out to start the game. Just develop your pieces and fight for the center.

O-O tucks your king away safely — always good. The engine liked ...d6 first to fight the e5 pawn, but castling is sensible.
White takes on f4, winning back the gambit pawn. The game is roughly level now; just keep developing.
Nc6 develops your last minor piece — exactly right, this is the best move.
White plays Bd3, quietly pointing the bishop at your h7 pawn near your king. Watch that diagonal.
d6 challenges the e5 pawn, but ...d5 was cleaner and would block that dangerous bishop. Keep an eye on h7.
White plays Bxh7+, a sacrifice that does NOT work here — a real gift to you. Just take it with Kxh7; the attack falls short and you win a whole bishop.
Kxh7 grabs the bishop. Correct — you are now up a piece.
White checks with Ng5+, but it's just a bluff with no follow-up. Simply step the king back.
Kg8 returns your king to safety. Well played.
White plays Qh4, lining up the queen and knight to threaten your h7 square. You must defend — ...Bf5 covers everything and keeps you winning.
Re8 was a serious slip because it ignores the danger to your king. The saving move was ...Bf5: it guards the key squares and shuts down White's attack.
White checks with Qh7+ and pushes your king into the open. Your king must walk forward — Kf8.
Kf8 is forced; the king has to march out. Keep it as safe as you can.
Another check, Qh8+, herding your king further. Keep walking — Ke7.
Ke7 is the only square. Try to find shelter and counterplay fast.
White grabs the g7 pawn with check pressure. Your king is exposed, so look for a defending move.
Rf8 tries to shield the king, but ...Nxe5 was stronger — it brings a piece back to defend and grabs a pawn. Defense is urgent here.
White castles, instantly aiming the rook at your weak f7 square. That square is now the main danger.
White plays Rxf7+, the rook sacrifice that forces mate. The f7 square has fallen.
Rxf7 is forced — you have to take the rook. Sadly it does not help.

Qxf7# is checkmate. The whole finish came from the loose f7 square — guarding it earlier (with ...Bf5 or ...Be6) was the key. You played a good game up a piece; just slow down and defend your king when it gets exposed.
You start with the king pawn. A great way to grab the center.
Black plays the French style with a pawn to e6. They keep things solid. Just keep building your center.
You push d4 and now you own a big center. Perfect plan.
Black plays b6 to put the bishop on the long line, but this is slow. You got a small edge — keep developing.
You bring the knight out to f3. Calm and good development.

You take the d5 pawn. Clean and best. Now Black must spend time winning it back while you get your rooks active.
Black grabs the edge with the knight to b4 instead of taking back. A little awkward for them. Bring a rook to c1 and keep pressing.
Your queen comes out to b3, aiming at f7 again — the same weak spot from your Italian bishop. A rook to e1 was a hair sharper, but this is fine and active.
Black's queen blocks on d6. This was a small slip by Black. Bring your other rook into the game and keep building pressure in the center.
You bring the rook to e1, putting it on the open file. Great — rooks love open lines and this points right at Black's position.
Black finally takes your d5 pawn with the knight. Now jump your knight to e4 — it hits Black's pieces and gets very active.
You leap the knight to e4, attacking Black's knight on f6. Strong and best — your knight is now a monster in the middle.
Big mistake by Black! Retreating the queen drops material. Punish it now: take on f6 with check (Nxf6+) — you win the f6 knight cleanly.
You take on f6 with check, winning the knight as planned. Perfect. You are now up a piece — keep your eyes open for more.
Black takes back with the knight. Fine. Now jump your knight to e5, a powerful central square that eyes f7.
Your knight lands on e5, staring at the f7 square near Black's king — the same weak spot from way back in the opening. Excellent piece.
Black grabs your d4 pawn with the queen. Let it go — you have a winning attack. The strongest hit is Bxf7+, but your knight plan also works.
You take f7 with the knight, going for the king. The engine slightly preferred the bishop check first, but you are clearly winning. Stay accurate.
Black slides the knight to g4. Don't panic. Calm moves keep your big advantage; just keep your king safe and your pieces coordinated.
You give a knight check on h6. It works, though Nd8+ was even cleaner. Still, Black's king is getting chased and you are winning easily.
Black's king steps to h8 into the corner. Good for you — the king is trapped on the edge. Keep checking and improving your pieces.
You check again with the knight on f7. Fine. (Note: this lets Black move the king back, so it's a repeat dance — but your position is still winning.)
Black's king returns to g8. You're still completely winning. Now stop the checks, bring your rook to e2, and use your extra piece to finish.
A great start. You take the center with your pawn and open lines for your bishop and queen.
Your opponent copies you and grabs the center too. This is a fair, even fight. Just keep developing your pieces.
Nice. Your knight comes out and puts pressure on the black pawn in the center.
Black defends the attacked pawn with a knight. This is normal. Keep bringing out your pieces.
You develop your other knight. The book move was Bc4 aiming at f7, but this is fine and very close to equal.
Black's bishop pins your knight to nothing important here, but it sets up to trade. You can just continue developing.
You ask the bishop a question. The slightly sharper Nd5 was an option, but a3 is okay and keeps things simple.
Black keeps the bishop on the long line instead of trading. No harm done. Carry on developing.
Good choice. Your bishop comes out and points right at the weak f7 square near the black king.
Black develops a knight and attacks your center pawn. This is normal; you have ways to keep it defended.
Too early. Better was Nd5, jumping to a strong central square. Ng5 looks scary at f7 but it can be chased away and loses time. Lesson: don't rush one piece forward before the others are out.
A mistake by Black. The right move was to castle. Now your pawn can take on d5 and win material. Take it!
Perfect. You grab the pawn and your pawn now attacks the black knight on c6. Strong move.
A big blunder. Black should have moved the attacked knight to d4. Now play dxc6 — your pawn takes the knight and you win a whole piece.
Exactly right. You take the knight and win a piece. Well done staying alert.
Black grabs your knight back on g5 to even the trade. This was Black's best try. You are still up material.
Good. Your queen comes out with energy and eyes the black king and the f7 area.
Black offers to trade queens. The cleaner move for Black was to castle. You don't have to trade — you have a strong pawn on c6.
You take the pawn and your pawn is now one step from becoming a queen. The very precise Bd5 also worked, but this is fully fine.
A blunder. Black should have taken your strong pawn. Now play bxc8=Q+ — your pawn promotes to a new queen WITH check and you win the rook. Don't miss the promotion!
You missed the big chance. Better was bxc8=R+, promoting your pawn with check first. Trading queens is okay, but promoting won much more. Lesson: always look at a pawn that can promote.
Black recaptures. This is forced and normal. You still have that dangerous pawn sitting on b7.

A serious miss. You should have played bxc8=Q+ — promote the b7 pawn to a queen with check! Castling is safe, but you left a free new queen on the board. Lesson: a pawn on the 7th rank is gold — promote it.
Black blocks the promotion path instead of taking the pawn. Black's best was Bxb7. Your pawn is still alive — keep watching it.
Good. Your bishop swings to a6 and keeps an eye on things. This was the engine's top move.
Black pushes a pawn at your king to open lines. Be careful here — your king safety matters now.
Risky. Better was d4 to keep things closed. Taking with the pawn opens your king and lets Black's knight jump in. Lesson: think twice before opening files near your own king.
Black's knight jumps to a strong square and attacks your weak pawn. Watch for it hopping in with check.
Off track. Better was Kg2 to tuck your king safe. The knight on b5 wanders to the edge and does little. Lesson: in trouble, fix your king first.
As warned, the knight takes your pawn with check. You must move your king. This is the cost of opening lines earlier.
Good, you move your king to the corner. This was the right square. Stay calm and hold things together.
Black's bishop comes to a strong central spot. Castling was a touch better for Black. Keep defending.
A big mistake. Better was c4, hitting the bishop. Giving a knight check on c7 just loses the knight, because the bishop takes it for free. Lesson: check that a checking piece is actually safe.
Black takes your knight, as expected. You are now worse off from that trade. Stay focused and fight on.
Good fighting move. Your pawn attacks the black bishop and tries to win it back.
Correct, you recapture and keep material even on that side. Good, steady play.

You missed it. Better was Re1+, giving check with your rook like in the punishing line. Hiding the king on g1 lets Black escape and even take your bishop. Lesson: when the opponent blunders, look for a check first.
Great start! You take the center with the king's pawn. This is the most popular and best first move.
The opponent copies you and grabs the center too. This is normal — keep developing your pieces.

They copy you again with a mirror bishop. The position is even and calm.
You castle and tuck your king safe in the corner. A smart, healthy move.
They develop their knight and eye your center. Normal — you can just keep building with d3.

Small mistake. The knight jumps at f7 but it gets chased away and wastes time. Better was d3, keeping your strong bishop and a solid setup. Lesson: don't attack early if the attack can be kicked back.
They push a pawn to hit your bishop and break free. Good for them — just take the pawn with exd5.
Nice. You grab the pawn back and keep things balanced. The right reply.
Mistake by them — the knight goes to the edge to chase your bishop, but edge knights are weak. Punish with Bb5+, a check that wins time and keeps your bishop.
Mistake. Better was Bb5+ first. Why: the check gains time and keeps your good bishop, while Bb3 lets them swap it off later. Lesson: when you have a check that helps, look at it first.
They poke your knight with a pawn. You must move the knight to safety.
Good. The knight retreats to a safe, useful square. Calm and correct.
They push the pawn again to bother your knight. You need a plan to push back.
A bit slow. Better was d4, hitting their bishop and opening lines for you. The rook move just waits. Lesson: meet a pawn push by striking the center yourself.
They castle and get their king safe. Normal — nothing to fear yet.

Big mistake. The knight lands where it gets hit by their bishop, losing time and the thread of the game. Much better was d4, gaining space and attacking. Lesson: don't place a piece where it can be kicked for free.
Their bishop attacks your knight and grabs a strong central spot. You must deal with the threat.
Inaccurate. Better was d3, calmly defending. The knight wandering here costs you. Stay solid instead.
Big blunder by them — the queen grabs a pawn but walks into a fork. Punish with Ne3, hitting the queen and gaining a tempo.
You missed the cleaner Nc3 hitting the queen. Still, Nb6 also jumps at the queen and the corner. Lesson: when you see one good attack, check if a second one is even better.
Huge blunder! They tucked the king away but left the queen hanging. Win it right now with Nxd5 — you take the whole queen for free.
Excellent! You snap up the queen. This is a winning material lead — now play safe and simple.
Their bishop attacks your queen. Just move it to a safe square.
Awkward. Better was Ne3, keeping things tidy and defended. The rook move walks into trouble. Lesson: when ahead, choose the calm, solid square.
They double rooks on the open file to make pressure. Stay alert and trade pieces to ease it.
Good. You take the knight and keep your big material lead. Simple is best.
They recapture but wreck their own pawns near the king. Great for you — those weak pawns are targets.
Fine. You challenge their advanced pawn. A reasonable move.

Mistake. Better was to trade rooks first with Rxe8. Why: cxd3 lets their bishop win your rook. Lesson: when a piece is attacked, deal with it before grabbing pawns.
Their bishop takes your rook. You should win it back.
Big mistake! After Qxe2 their rook takes your queen. Better was Qd2, keeping the queen safe. This throws away your winning lead. Lesson: before a recapture, check if you get taken right back.
Their rook takes your queen. Now the game is roughly level again — keep fighting.
Small slip. Bd2 was a touch better. Your king step is okay though.
They grab a pawn with the rook. Stay active and look for your own targets.
Inaccurate. Better was Be3, keeping your bishop active and safe. Grabbing the pawn helps them more.

Mistake. Better was Be3. The knight to the edge is passive and gets attacked. Lesson: keep knights near the center, not the rim.
They take your bishop with the rook. You can win the rook back with a2xb3.
Inaccurate — axb3 would simply take the rook back. The rook move is a bit slow. Take the free material when offered.
They take your knight. Material is messy now, but your rook is active — use it.
Good. Your rook grabs a pawn and gets very active behind their position. Strong rook play.
They step the king aside. Keep your rook munching pawns and making threats.
Okay, you grab a pawn with check, though Bd2 was a touch better. Active rook keeps the pressure.
Their king walks out into the open. Keep checking and chasing to stay active.
Mistake. Better was Bc1, keeping the bishop safe. This square invites a trade that helps them. Lesson: keep your bishop on safe diagonals.

You push your passed pawn forward, a small plan. Bb2 was slightly better, but pushing is fine.

Terrible blunder — this hangs your bishop and the game is now lost. Better was h3, keeping the bishop. They will simply take it next. Lesson: before every move, check if the piece you move can just be captured.
They grab a pawn (and your bishop falls soon). The position is now very hard for you.
